title: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis with R/Bioconductor
text:
What
This course will introduce biologists and bioinformaticians to the field of single-cell RNA sequencing. We will cover a range of software and analysis workflows that extend over the spectrum from the best practices in the filtering scRNA-seq data to the downstream analysis of cell clusters and temporal ordering. This course will help the attendees gain accurate insights in pre-processing, analysis and interpretation of scRNA-seq data.
We will start by introducing general concepts about single-cell RNA-sequencing. From there, we will then continue to describe the main analysis steps to go from raw sequencing data to processed and usable data. We will present classical analysis workflows, their output and the possible paths to investigate downstream of this.
Throughout the workshop, bash tools and R/Bioconductor packages will be used to analyse datasets and learn new approaches.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis with R/Bioconductor

When

Dates of the 2026 edition: to be announced. Classes run from 14:00 to 20:00 (Paris time), over five days.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis with R/Bioconductor
text:
Where
This course will be held online. All the hands-on labs run in the cloud, on the Bioconductor Orchestra platform: each participant gets their own RStudio session, in their web browser, started from the Docker image built from this book.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis with R/Bioconductor
text:
How
The course is structured in modules over five days. Each day will include formal lectures covering the key concepts required to understand scRNA-seq analysis. The remainder of each day will consist in practical hands-on sessions focusing on analysis of scRNA-seq data. These sessions will involve a combination of both mirroring exercises with the instructor to demonstrate a skill, as well as applying these skills on your own to complete individual exercises. During and after each exercise, interpretation of results will be discussed as a group.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis with R/Bioconductor
text:
Who
The course will be mostly beneficial to those who have, or will shortly have, scRNA-seq data ready to analyse.
The material is suitable both for experimentalists who want to learn more about data-analysis as well as computational biologists who want to learn about scRNA-seq methods.
Examples demonstrated in this course can be applied to any experimental protocol or biological system.
The requirements for this course are:

Working knowledge of Unix / command line interface (managing files, running programs, reading manuals!). Basic bash commands (cd, ls, ...) and CLI usage will not be covered in this course. We advice attendees to not register if they lack fundamental experience in CLI.
Programming experience in R (writing a function, basic I/O operations, variable types, using packages). Bioconductor experience is a plus.
Familiarity with next-generation sequencing data and its analyses (using alignment and quantification tools for bulk sequencing data)

See the Prerequisites page for refresher material.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis with R/Bioconductor
text:
Why
At the end of this course, you should be able to:

Understand the pros/cons of different single-cell RNA-seq methods
Process and QC of scRNA-seq data
Normalize scRNA-seq data
Correct for batch effects
Visualise the data and applying dimensionality reduction
Perform cell clustering and annotation
Perform differential gene expression analysis
Infer cell trajectory and pseudotime, and perform temporal differential expression

Throughout the course, we will also have a focus on reproducible research, documented content and interactive reports.

title: Getting started
text:
During the workshop: the Orchestra platform
All the labs of this workshop run in RStudio, in a Linux environment providing R, Bioconductor, all the R packages, command-line tools and datasets we will use. This environment is distributed as a Docker image, built automatically from this book:
👉 ghcr.io/js2264/scrnaseqphysalia2026 🐳
There are two ways to use it: in the cloud, on the Orchestra platform (this is what we will do during the workshop), or on your own computer.
Orchestra is an open-source platform, supported by the Bioconductor community, which runs workshop environments in the cloud. Each participant gets their own, isolated RStudio session, in their web browser: there is nothing to install on your computer.

title: Getting started
text:
Open the Orchestra dashboard: the link will be given by your instructors at the beginning of the workshop.
Sign in with a Google account (any Google account works, either a personal Gmail address or an institutional account backed by Google).
Pick the “Single-cell RNA-seq analysis with R/Bioconductor (Physalia 2026)” workshop from the catalog and click on Launch. Starting the session can take a few minutes the first time (the status moves from Pending to Starting to Ready).
When it’s Ready, click on Open: RStudio opens in a new tab, already logged in.







WarningYour session is temporary!



Every session has a time limit, shown as a countdown on its card in the dashboard (you can extend it by clicking on +1h). When a session expires (or when you terminate it), everything in it is removed, including the files you created.
Download anything you want to keep (scripts, notebooks, results) before the end of each day: in RStudio, tick the files in the Files pane, then click on More > Export....

title: Getting started
section: After the workshop: on your own computer
text:
After the workshop: on your own computer
If Docker is installed on your computer, you can start exactly the same environment locally. In a terminal:



bash

docker run \
    --volume ~/scRNAseq_Physalia_2026:/home/rstudio/work \
    -e PASSWORD=physalia \
    -p 8787:8787 \
    ghcr.io/js2264/scrnaseqphysalia2026:devel


Then open http://localhost:8787 in your web browser, and log in with user rstudio and password physalia. The ~/scRNAseq_Physalia_2026 folder of your computer is available in RStudio as ~/work: save your files there to keep them after the container stops.






TipMemory requirements



Some labs load fairly large datasets in memory: we recommend giving at least 8 GB of RAM to Docker (in Docker Desktop: Settings > Resources).


Alternatively, you can install all the packages used in this workshop in your own R installation (R >= 4.6 and a current version of Bioconductor are required):



R

install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("js2264/scRNAseq_Physalia_2026", dependencies = TRUE)

title: Getting started
text:
RStudio
RStudio offers a graphical interface to facilitate the interaction between a user and an underlying programming language (this is sometimes called IDE, or integrated development environment). It can be very useful when a user is not necessarily proficent with command line-based computing.
Don’t forget, you can run a bash terminal from within RStudio! This may come handy if you want to process some data with command-line tools (e.g. seqkit, samtools or cellranger), for example. To do this, simply go to Tools > Terminal > New terminal: a new Terminal tab opens next to the R console. You should now be in your own home directory (~).

title: Getting started
text:
Datasets
The labs download public datasets from GEO, ENA, 10x Genomics or Bioconductor’s ExperimentHub, using BiocFileCache (or the dedicated data packages): a dataset is only downloaded the first time it is requested, then read from a local cache. The datasets used in the R labs are already cached in the Docker image, so they are immediately available in your workshop session.

title: Prerequisites
text:
Knowledge
The course is intended for those who have basic familiarity with Unix and the R scripting language.
We will also assume that you are familiar with mapping and analyzing bulk RNA-seq data as well as with the commonly available computational tools.

title: 3  Lab 1: Familiarizing yourself with the workshop environment
text:
3.1 Connect to RStudio Server
Most of single-cell RNA-seq analysis takes place either in python or in R. Here, we focus on how to leverage R to investigate scRNAseq data. RStudio is an IDE (Integrated Development Environment, in other words: a nice graphical interface to run R-related commands).
For this workshop, every participant gets their own RStudio Server session, running in the cloud from the Docker image built from this book. Follow the steps described in Getting started to launch it from the Orchestra platform: a new tab opens in your browser with RStudio already logged in.
Notice how when you log in RStudio, there are multiple panels. Familiarize yourself with the different panels.
The interactive R console is generally found in the bottom left corner of RStudio (though it may be in another corner sometimes). All the rest (history panel, environment panel, directory explorer panel, editor panel) are extra features provided by RStudio.
crumbs: 3  Lab 1: Familiarizing yourself with the workshop environment

title: 3  Lab 1: Familiarizing yourself with the workshop environment
text:
TipSome useful commands in R:



Within the R console, you can safely use R-dedicated commands. Do you know the most common ones? The semantics are a different from the terminal commands you may be used to…



R

getwd() # equivalent of `pwd` in terminal
dir.create('~/data/') # equivalent of `mkdir ~/data/` in terminal
setwd("~/data/") # equivalent of `cd ~/data/` in terminal
list.files("~/data/") # equivalent of `ls` in terminal
download.file("...") # equivalent of `wget ...` in terminal
crumbs: 3  Lab 1: Familiarizing yourself with the workshop environment

title: 3  Lab 1: Familiarizing yourself with the workshop environment
text:
3.2 Use a terminal within RStudio
A general issue with bioinformatic analyses stems from the fact that nobody works in the same environment:

Are you working on Mac? Linux? Windows?
Do you have a lot of computational power? Perhaps a GPU card?
Are you connected to the Internet? With a fast connection? Are you working behind a proxy?
Which versions of R, Bioconductor and of each package are installed?

To ensure that we are all working in the same environment, we all run the same Docker image. A Docker image is a frozen, self-contained Linux system: it ships a given version of R, Bioconductor, every R package and every command-line tool used in this workshop, and even the datasets used in the labs. Each participant runs their own copy of this image (a container) in the cloud, so:


Everybody gets exactly the same software, down to package versions;

Your session is yours: you can install, modify or delete files without affecting anyone else;

Your session is temporary: download the files you want to keep before the end of the workshop!

The easiest way to launch bash commands from a terminal is to do it through RStudio: You can open up a terminal directly from within RStudio as follows: go to Tools > Terminal > New terminal. This should open up a new tab in the bottom left corner (next to the R console).






WarningR console versus terminal:



From here onwards, be sure you completely understand the difference between “R console” and “terminal (or shell)”. They are entirely different things, and can be both accessed within RStudio. It is crucial you understand the difference between the two to not get confused for the rest of the course.
crumbs: 3  Lab 1: Familiarizing yourself with the workshop environment

title: 3  Lab 1: Familiarizing yourself with the workshop environment
text:
3.3 Basic terminal commands
One can list files, download files, check help pages, …, just like in R.

Check the your present directory




bash

pwd



Check history




bash

history



put history into a history.txt file




bash

history > history.txt



make a new folder called data




bash

mkdir ~/data



Go to the new data directory




bash

cd ~/data



move history.txt file into data directory




bash

mv ../history.txt ./



check manual page of wget command (hit q to exit)




bash

man wget



check specific help for samtools command and subcommands




bash

samtools --help
samtools view --help



redirect the help output into a file called samtools-view-help.txt





bash

samtools view --help > samtools-view-help.txt



Download a file from Internet with wget





bash

wget https://cf.10xgenomics.com/supp/cell-exp/cellranger-tiny-bcl-1.2.0.tar.gz



List all files in a folder




bash

ls -lh ~/data/








TipTip



Download the git repository for this course from GitHub:



bash

git clone https://github.com/js2264/scRNAseq_Physalia_2026.git


This downloads the repository for this course to your home folder in your workshop session. To get it on your local computer (to save the lectures and exercises), go to the GitHub repo page, click on the green Code button, then Download ZIP. Beware, the download may take a significant time based on your internet connection (~100 MB).

title: 3  Lab 1: Familiarizing yourself with the workshop environment
text:
3.4 Single-cell RNA-seq datasets

“This is a course about single-cell RNA-seq analysis, after all, so where is my data?”

Ok, “your” data is (most likely) yet to be sequenced! Or maybe you’re interested in digging already existing databases!
The Human Cell Atlas data portal and the CZ CELLxGENE Discover portal are probably good places to start digging, if you are interested in mammal-related studies. For instance, let’s say I am interested in epididymis differentiation. Boom: here is an entry from the HCA focusing on epididymis: link to HCA data portal.

3.4.1 Raw fastq reads from GEO
Here is the link to the actual paper studying epididymis: An atlas of human proximal epididymis reveals cell-specific functions and distinct roles for CFTR.







NoteQuestion



Find and check out the corresponding GEO entries for this study. What type of sequencing data is available?






Tip



Here is the link to the GEO page: link.












NoteQuestion



Can you find links to download the raw data from this paper?



There are several ways to find this information, e.g. ffq command line tool, the web-based sra-explorer page (here), or the ENA browser. You generally will need the GEO corresponding ID or SRA project ID (e.g. SRPxxxxxx…).







NoteQuestion



The ffq tool from the Pachter lab is already installed in your workshop session. Check ffq help and try fetching metadata for the GSE ID GSE148963.






TipInstalling ffq on your own machine



ffq is a python package, available from PyPI:



bash

pip install ffq











NoteAnswer








bash

ffq --help
ffq -t GSE GSE148963 > GSE148963_search.txt
head -n 30 GSE148963_search.txt
















NoteQuestion



Can you find the links to raw data associated with the GSE148963 GEO ID?







NoteAnswer





You can use a grep command: grep returns the lines which match a given pattern (e.g. a link…)!



bash

grep 'ftp://' GSE148963_search.txt


And with a bit of sed magick…



bash

grep 'ftp://' GSE148963_search.txt | sed 's,.*ftp:,ftp:,' | sed 's,".*,,' | grep ".fastq" > GSE148963_fastqlist.txt
## `ffq` looks through GEO repository to fing metadata associated with the `GSE148963` entry (including downloading links)
## grep 'ftp://' recovers the text lines that contain downloading links
## the `sed` commands clean up the text lines
## the `wget` command downloads locally the links listed in the generated file (GSE148963_fastqlist.txt)
# wget -i GSE148963_fastqlist.txt ## Do not run, it would take too long...


The ENA also directly serves download links for any run accession:



bash

curl -s "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/filereport?accession=SRR11575369&result=read_run&fields=fastq_ftp,fastq_bytes,read_count"
















NoteQuestion



The full fastq files for a single run of this study weigh ~35 GB each… Let’s only download the first 25,000 reads of the SRR11575369 run (sample AXH009), by streaming the file from the ENA and stopping after 100,000 lines. Have a look at it!







NoteAnswer








bash

mkdir -p ~/data && cd ~/data
for READ in 1 2; do
    curl -s https://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/fastq/SRR115/069/SRR11575369/SRR11575369_${READ}.fastq.gz \
        | zcat 2>/dev/null \
        | head -n 100000 \
        | gzip > SRR11575369_${READ}.fq.gz
done
zcat SRR11575369_1.fq.gz | head -n 12
















NoteQuestion



Try and understand the structure of the fq.gz file. What is the meaning of each line? What is the difference between the _1 and _2 files?
How many reads are there in the fq.gz file? And how long are they? Can you get a summary of what is in this file? All of these questions can be quickly answered using the seqkit tool:







NoteAnswer








bash

seqkit --help
seqkit stats --help
seqkit stats ~/data/SRR11575369_*.fq.gz










3.4.2 Processed count matrices
Many times, researchers will provide a filtered count matrix when they publish scRNAseq experiments (along with mandatory raw fastq data, of course). It’s way lighter than fastq reads, and you can go ahead with downstream analyses a lot quicker. So how do you get these matrices? Human Cell Atlas Consortium provides many processed datasets. For instance, in our case, the A single cell atlas of the human proximal epididymis reveals cell-type specific functions and distinct roles for CFTR (Leir et al, 2020) study is available at the following link.
GEO also provides access to both raw and processed files.







NoteQuestion



Find GEO-hosted processed files for the Leir et al study.







NoteAnswer





Check the Geo Dataset search page.
Search for Leir 2020 CFTF. You should find the following entry.
Scrolling down to the bottom of the page, there is a box labelled “Supplementary data”. Each sample (GSM...) also has its own supplementary files: for instance, the processed files for sample AXH009 are listed on the GSM4486714 page.




Download and check the content of the count matrix, the genes and the barcodes files.
What type of information does each file contain? How is it formatted? is it easily imported in R?







NoteAnswer








bash

cd ~/data
URL=https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/samples/GSM4486nnn/GSM4486714/suppl
for FILE in matrix.mtx genes.tsv barcodes.tsv; do
    wget ${URL}/GSM4486714_AXH009_${FILE}.gz
done
ls -lh GSM4486714_AXH009_*
zcat GSM4486714_AXH009_genes.tsv.gz | head
zcat GSM4486714_AXH009_barcodes.tsv.gz | head
zcat GSM4486714_AXH009_matrix.mtx.gz | head


These three files are the standard output of cellranger (a “Matrix Market” sparse matrix, see Lab 2): the .mtx file only lists the non-zero entries of the count matrix, one per line, as <gene index> <cell index> <count>, after a 3-line header. The genes and barcodes files give the names of the rows and of the columns of the matrix. We will see how to import them in R in Lab 3.





How many cells were sequenced? How many genes were counted?
Is it easy to interpret the count matrix? Why is it in such format?
Comment on the file sizes between processed count matrix files and raw reads.

title: 4  Lab 2: From .bcl to count matrix
text:
4.1 Demultiplexing sequencing data with cellranger mkfastq
Navigate to your terminal in RStudio.
Go to the cellranger mkfastq page and read the Overview.
For this workshop, we are going to look at a toy dataset provided by 10x Genomics: cellranger-tiny-bcl-1.2.0. It comes with a samplesheet file, cellranger-tiny-bcl-simple-1.2.0.csv, which contains the sample information.
bash

mkdir -p ~/data/data_wrangling && cd ~/data/data_wrangling
wget https://cf.10xgenomics.com/supp/cell-exp/cellranger-tiny-bcl-1.2.0.tar.gz
wget https://cf.10xgenomics.com/supp/cell-exp/cellranger-tiny-bcl-simple-1.2.0.csv
tar -xzf cellranger-tiny-bcl-1.2.0.tar.gz
Now we can demultiplex our bcl files by running the following command in the terminal. To do that, we will use the cellranger mkfastq command.
bash

cellranger mkfastq --help
The output folders can be viewed by running the ls command:
bash

ls -l ~/data/data_wrangling/tiny-bcl/outs/fastq_path/H35KCBCXY/test_sample
Open the html file tiny-bcl/outs/fastq_path/Reports/html/index.html by navigating to the file in RStudio, using the Files Tab. When you click on the file, select the option to View in Web Browser. Take some time to explore the demultiplexed outputs.
crumbs: 4  Lab 2: From .bcl to count matrix

title: 4  Lab 2: From .bcl to count matrix
text:
NoteQuestion



Go to the Terminal tab in your RStudio and take a look at the 10x samplesheet .csv file







NoteAnswer








bash

cat ~/data/data_wrangling/cellranger-tiny-bcl-simple-1.2.0.csv


Lane,Sample,Index
1,test_sample,SI-P03-C9














NoteQuestion



Next, explore the contents of the sequencing directory:







NoteAnswer








bash

ls -l ~/data/data_wrangling/cellranger-tiny-bcl-1.2.0


total 28
drwxr-xr-x 2 rstudio rstudio 4096 Nov 12  2016 Config
drwxr-xr-x 3 rstudio rstudio 4096 Nov 12  2016 Data
drwxr-xr-x 2 rstudio rstudio 4096 Nov 12  2016 InterOp
-rw-r--r-- 1 rstudio rstudio   48 Nov 12  2016 RTAComplete.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 rstudio rstudio  673 Nov 12  2016 RunInfo.xml
-rw-r--r-- 1 rstudio rstudio 5366 Nov 12  2016 runParameters.xml
















NoteQuestion



What is the purpose of --id, --run, and --csv arguments ?
Choose these arguments wisely and execute the command to demultiplex the sequencing data.







NoteAnswer








bash

cd ~/data/data_wrangling
cellranger mkfastq \

4.2 Generating gene count matrices with cellranger count

Go to the cellranger count algorithm overview and read the section on Alignment (Read Trimming, Genome Alignment, MAPQ adjustment, Transcriptome Alignment, UMI Counting).
In bash, the cellranger count command is used to generate gene count matrices from the demultiplexed reads.



bash

cellranger count --help


Now, we will generate a gene count matrix for the test_sample reads using cellranger count and the refdata-gex-mm10-2020-A transcriptome reference provided by 10x Genomics.







NoteQuestion



What is the purpose of the --id, --transcriptome, --fastqs, --sample, and --create-bam arguments?







NoteAnswer








bash

## Change this path to the location of the pre-built reference in your session
REF=~/data/refdata-gex-mm10-2020-A
cd ~/data/data_wrangling
cellranger count \
    --id counts \
    --transcriptome ${REF} \
    --fastqs tiny-bcl/outs/fastq_path/H35KCBCXY/test_sample \
    --sample test_sample \
    --create-bam true

6.1 Installing packages in R
Or, in other words: “how do I install this or that brand new cutting-edge fancy package?”
R works with packages, available from different sources:
Let’s start by going over package installation.
Package help pages are available at different places, depending on their source. That being said, there is a place I like to go to easily find information related to most packages:
https://rdrr.io/
For instance, check out Revelio package help pages.

title: 6  Lab 3: Introduction to R/Bioconductor
text:
“Hey, I’ve heard so many good things about this piece of software, it’s called ‘slingshot’? Heard of it? I really want to try it out on my dataset!!”





CRAN, the R developer team and official package provider: CRAN.

Bioconductor, another package provider, with a primary focus on genomic-related packages: Bioconductor.
Other unofficial sources, such as GitHub.









NoteQuestion



Install mgcv, HCAData and revelio packages. Each of these three packages is available from a different source:


mgcv is a CRAN package

HCAData is a Bioconductor package

revelio is a GitHub package








NoteAnswer





BiocManager::install() is the recommended way to install packages for a given version of Bioconductor: it installs packages from Bioconductor, from CRAN, and from GitHub (given a "<user>/<repo>" name), while making sure that all of them are compatible with each other.



R

install.packages('mgcv')
BiocManager::install('HCAData')
BiocManager::install('danielschw188/Revelio')


You can check which version of Bioconductor you are using, and whether any installed package is out-of-date or too recent for it:



R

BiocManager::version()
BiocManager::valid()















TipPackages in your workshop session



All the packages used in this workshop are already installed in your workshop session (and in the Docker image it is started from).






What is this package designed for?
What are its main functions? What type of input does it require?

title: 6  Lab 3: Introduction to R/Bioconductor
text:
6.2 Basic R and Bioconductor classes
While CRAN is a repository of general-purpose packages, Bioconductor is the greatest source of analytical tools, data and workflows dedicated to genomic projects in R. Read more about Bioconductor to fully understand how it builds up on top of R general features, especially with the specific classes it introduces.
The two main concepts behind Bioconductor’s success are the non-redundant classes of objects it provides and their inter-operability. Huber et al., Nat. Methods 2015 summarizes it well.

6.2.1 Important R concepts:

6.2.1.1 tibble tables:
tibbles are built on the fundamental data.frame objects. They follow “tidy” concepts, all gathered in a common tidyverse. This set of key concepts help general data investigation and data visualization through a set of associated packages such as ggplot2.



R

library(tidyverse)
##  ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ───────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
##  ✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
##  ✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
##  ✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
##  ✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
##  ✔ purrr     1.2.2     
##  ── Conflicts ─────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
##  ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
##  ✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
##  ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors
dat <- tibble(
    x = 1:5,
    y = 1,
    z = x ^ 2 + y,
    class = c('a', 'a', 'b', 'b', 'c')
)
dat
##  # A tibble: 5 × 4
##        x     y     z class
##    <int> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>
##  1     1     1     2 a    
##  2     2     1     5 a    
##  3     3     1    10 b    
##  4     4     1    17 b    
##  5     5     1    26 c



Import a text file into tibbles

tibbles can be created from text files (or Excel files) using the readr package (part of tidyverse). We will read the list of genes quantified by cellranger in the AXH009 sample from Leir et al. (see Lab 1).
Rather than downloading the file by hand, we use BiocFileCache: it downloads a file the first time it is requested, stores it in a local cache, and simply returns the path to the cached copy afterwards.



R

library(BiocFileCache)
##  Loading required package: dbplyr
##  
##  Attaching package: 'dbplyr'
##  The following objects are masked from 'package:dplyr':
##  
##      ident, sql, sql_escape_ident, sql_escape_string
##  OpenTelemetry error: there is no package called 'otelsdk'
##  OpenTelemetry error: there is no package called 'otelsdk'
bfc <- BiocFileCache(ask = FALSE)
genes_file <- bfcrpath(bfc, "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/samples/GSM4486nnn/GSM4486714/suppl/GSM4486714_AXH009_genes.tsv.gz")
##  adding rname 'https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/samples/GSM4486nnn/GSM4486714/suppl/GSM4486714_AXH009_genes.tsv.gz'
genes_file
##                                                                       BFC1 
##  "/opt/R-cache/R/BiocFileCache/1c51342f822_GSM4486714_AXH009_genes.tsv.gz"
genes <- read_tsv(genes_file, col_names = c('ID', 'Symbol'))
##  Rows: 32738 Columns: 2
##  ── Column specification ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
##  Delimiter: "\t"
##  chr (2): ID, Symbol
##  
##  ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
##  ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
genes

##    ID              Symbol      
##    <chr>           <chr>       
##  1 ENSG00000243485 MIR1302-10  
##  2 ENSG00000237613 FAM138A     
##  3 ENSG00000186092 OR4F5

##  5 ENSG00000239945 RP11-34P13.8

6.2.1.2 Handling of tibbles:
tibbles can be readily “sliced” (i.e. selecting rows by number/name), “filtered” (i.e. selecting rows by condition) and columns can be “selected”. All these operations are performed using verbs (most of them provided by the dplyr package, part of tidyverse).



R

slice(genes, 1:4)
##  # A tibble: 4 × 2
##    ID              Symbol      
##    <chr>           <chr>       
##  1 ENSG00000243485 MIR1302-10  
##  2 ENSG00000237613 FAM138A     
##  3 ENSG00000186092 OR4F5       
##  4 ENSG00000238009 RP11-34P13.7
filter(genes, Symbol == 'CFTR')
##  # A tibble: 1 × 2
##    ID              Symbol
##    <chr>           <chr> 
##  1 ENSG00000001626 CFTR
filter(genes, grepl('^CCDC.*', Symbol))

##    ID              Symbol  
##    <chr>           <chr>   
##  1 ENSG00000162592 CCDC27

##  4 ENSG00000177868 CCDC23  
##  5 ENSG00000159214 CCDC24  
##  6 ENSG00000236624 CCDC163P

filter(genes, grepl('^CCDC.*', Symbol), grepl('.*5$', Symbol))

##  3 ENSG00000186092

##  5 ENSG00000239945

select(genes, ID)

##  3 ENSG00000186092

select(genes, matches('Sym.*'))

##    <chr>       
##  1 MIR1302-10  
##  2 FAM138A     
##  3 OR4F5       
##  4 RP11-34P13.7
##  5 RP11-34P13.8

Columns can also be quickly added/modified using the mutate verb.



R

mutate(genes, chr = sample(1:22, n(), replace = TRUE))
##  # A tibble: 32,738 × 3
##    ID              Symbol         chr
##    <chr>           <chr>        <int>
##  1 ENSG00000243485 MIR1302-10      16
##  2 ENSG00000237613 FAM138A         16
##  3 ENSG00000186092 OR4F5           15
##  4 ENSG00000238009 RP11-34P13.7    21
##  5 ENSG00000239945 RP11-34P13.8     3
##  6 ENSG00000237683 AL627309.1       9
##  # ℹ 32,732 more rows



6.2.1.3 |> pipe:
Actions on tibbles can be piped as a chain with |>, just like | pipes stdout as the stdin of the next command in bash. In this case, the first argument is always the output of the previous function and is ommited. Because tidyverse functions generally return a modified version of the input, pipping works remarkably well in such context.



R

read_tsv(genes_file, col_names = c('ID', 'Symbol')) |>
    mutate(chr = sample(1:22, n(), replace = TRUE)) |>
    filter(chr == 2, grepl('^CCDC.*', Symbol)) |>
    select(ID) |>
    slice_head(n = 3)
##  Rows: 32738 Columns: 2
##  ── Column specification ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
##  Delimiter: "\t"
##  chr (2): ID, Symbol
##  
##  ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
##  ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

##    ID             
##    <chr>          
##  1 ENSG00000144395
##  2 ENSG00000198865
##  3 ENSG00000203952



6.2.2 Important Bioconductor concepts:

6.2.2.1 SummarizedExperiment class:
The most fundamental class used to hold the content of large-scale quantitative analyses, such as counts of RNA-seq experiments, or high-throughput cytometry experiments or proteomics experiments.

Make sure you understand the structure of objects from this class. A dedicated workshop that I would recommend quickly going over is available here. Generally speaking, a SummarizedExperiment object contains matrix-like objects (the assays), with rows representing features (e.g. genes, transcripts, …) and each column representing a sample. Information specific to genes and samples are stored in “parallel” data frames, for example to store gene locations, tissue of expression, biotypes (for genes) or batch, generation date, or machine ID (for samples). On top of that, metadata are also stored in the object (to store description of a project, …).
An important difference with S3 list-like objects usually used in R is that most of the underlying data (organized in precisely structured "slots") is accessed using getter functions, rather than the familiar $ or [. Here are some important getters:


assay(), assays(): Extract matrix-like or list of matrix-like objects of identical dimensions. Since the objects are matrix-like, dim(), dimnames(), and 2-dimensional [, [<- methods are available.

colData(): Annotations on each column (as a DataFrame): usually, description of each sample

rowData(): Annotations on each row (as a DataFrame): usually, description of each gene

metadata(): List of unstructured metadata describing the overall content of the object.

Let’s dig into an example, with the airway dataset (provided by the airway package from Bioconductor).

6.2.2.2 GenomicRanges class (a.k.a. GRanges):
GenomicRanges are a type of IntervalRanges, they are useful to describe genomic intervals. Each entry in a GRanges object has a seqnames(), a start() and an end() coordinates, a strand(), as well as associated metadata (mcols()). They can be built from scratch using tibbles converted with makeGRangesFromDataFrame().



R

library(GenomicRanges)
gr <- read_tsv(genes_file, col_names = c('ID', 'Symbol')) |>
    mutate(
        chr = sample(1:22, n(), replace = TRUE),
        start = sample(1:1000, n(), replace = TRUE),
        end = sample(10000:20000, n(), replace = TRUE),
        strand = sample(c('-', '+'), n(), replace = TRUE)
    ) |>
    makeGRangesFromDataFrame(keep.extra.columns = TRUE)

title: 6  Lab 3: Introduction to R/Bioconductor
text:
6.3 CRAN & Bioconductor approaches to scRNAseq

6.3.1 scRNAseq in Bioconductor
For single-cell RNA-seq projects, Bioconductor has been introducting new classes and standards very rapidly in the past few years. Notably, several packages are increasingly becoming central for single-cell analysis:

SingleCellExperiment
scrapper
scater
scran
scuttle
bluster
batchelor
SingleR
DropletUtils
slingshot
tradeSeq
…

SingleCellExperiment is the fundamental class designed to contain single-cell (RNA-seq) data in Bioconductor ecosystem. It is a modified version of the SummarizedExperiment object, so most of the getters/setters are shared with this class.

Let’s load a dataset of mouse haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (Nestorowa et al., Blood 2016, doi: 10.1182/blood-2016-05-716480), distributed by the scRNAseq package, and normalize its counts.



R

library(SingleCellExperiment)
sce <- scRNAseq::fetchDataset("nestorowa-hsc-2016", "2024-04-18")

## Load the counts in memory, as a sparse matrix
counts(sce) <- as(counts(sce), "dgCMatrix")

## Compute normalized counts (more on this in the next labs!),
## and store them as a sparse matrix too
sce <- scrapper::normalizeRnaCounts.se(sce, more.norm.args = list(delayed = FALSE))
sce$label <- sce$broad
sce
##  class: SingleCellExperiment 
##  dim: 46078 1920 
##  metadata(0):
##  assays(2): counts logcounts
##  rownames(46078): ENSMUSG00000000001 ENSMUSG00000000003 ...
##    ENSMUSG00000107391 ENSMUSG00000107392
##  rowData names(0):
##  colnames(1920): HSPC_007 HSPC_013 ... Prog_852 Prog_810
##  colData names(11): gate broad ... sizeFactor label
##  reducedDimNames(1): diffusion
##  mainExpName: endogenous
##  altExpNames(2): ERCC FACS
class(sce)
##  [1] "SingleCellExperiment"
##  attr(,"package")
##  [1] "SingleCellExperiment"

6.3.2 scRNAseq in R
Seurat is another very popular ecosystem to investigate scRNAseq data. It is primarily developed and maintained by the Satija Lab. It originally begun as a single package aiming at encompassing “all” (most) aspects of scRNAseq analysis. However, it rapidly evolved in a much larger project, and now operates along with other “wrappers” and extensions. It also has a very extended support from the lab group. All in all, is provides a (somewhat) simple workflow to start investigating scRNAseq data.
It is important to chose one standard that you feel comfortable with yourself. Which standard provides the most intuitive approach for you? Do you prefer an “all-in-one, plug-n-play” workflow (Seurat-style), or a modular approach (Bioconductor-style)? Which documentation is easier to read for you, a central full-featured website with extensive examples (Seurat-style), or “programmatic”-style vignettes (Bioconductor-style)?
This course will mostly rely on Bioconductor-based methods, but sometimes use Seurat-based methods. In the absence of coordination of data structures, the next best solution is to write functions to coerce an object from a certain class to another class (i.e. Seurat to SingleCellExperiment, or vice-versa). Luckily, this is quite straightforward in R for these 2 data classes:



R

sce_seurat <- Seurat::as.Seurat(removeAltExps(sce))
sce
##  class: SingleCellExperiment 
##  dim: 46078 1920 
##  metadata(0):
##  assays(2): counts logcounts
##  rownames(46078): ENSMUSG00000000001 ENSMUSG00000000003 ...
##    ENSMUSG00000107391 ENSMUSG00000107392
##  rowData names(0):
##  colnames(1920): HSPC_007 HSPC_013 ... Prog_852 Prog_810
##  colData names(11): gate broad ... sizeFactor label
##  reducedDimNames(1): diffusion
##  mainExpName: endogenous
##  altExpNames(2): ERCC FACS
sce_seurat
##  An object of class Seurat 
##  46078 features across 1920 samples within 1 assay 
##  Active assay: endogenous (46078 features, 0 variable features)
##   2 layers present: counts, data
##   1 dimensional reduction calculated: diffusion
sce2 <- Seurat::as.SingleCellExperiment(sce_seurat)


Note that we had to remove the alternative experiments (altExps) before converting the object: Seurat stores each of them as an additional Assay, and cannot convert the FACS intensities, which are not counts.

6.4 Reading scRNAseq data







NoteQuestion



Try to load the processed 10X single-cell RNA-seq data of the AXH009 sample from Leir et al. (see Lab 1) into a SingleCellExperiment object using the DropletUtils package.






Tip



DropletUtils::read10xCounts() expects a folder containing three files named matrix.mtx.gz, barcodes.tsv.gz and features.tsv.gz (the names used by cellranger), or a .h5 file.









NoteAnswer








R

## Download the three files and put them in a folder, with cellranger names
url <- "https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/samples/GSM4486nnn/GSM4486714/suppl/GSM4486714_AXH009_"
AXH009_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "AXH009")
dir.create(AXH009_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
file.copy(bfcrpath(bfc, paste0(url, "matrix.mtx.gz")), file.path(AXH009_dir, "matrix.mtx.gz"))
##  adding rname 'https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/samples/GSM4486nnn/GSM4486714/suppl/GSM4486714_AXH009_matrix.mtx.gz'
##  [1] TRUE
file.copy(bfcrpath(bfc, paste0(url, "barcodes.tsv.gz")), file.path(AXH009_dir, "barcodes.tsv.gz"))
##  adding rname 'https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/samples/GSM4486nnn/GSM4486714/suppl/GSM4486714_AXH009_barcodes.tsv.gz'
##  [1] TRUE
file.copy(bfcrpath(bfc, paste0(url, "genes.tsv.gz")), file.path(AXH009_dir, "features.tsv.gz"))
##  [1] TRUE
list.files(AXH009_dir)
##  [1] "barcodes.tsv.gz" "features.tsv.gz" "matrix.mtx.gz"

## Import them as a SingleCellExperiment
sce <- DropletUtils::read10xCounts(AXH009_dir, col.names = TRUE)

Public single-cell RNA-seq data can be retrieved from within R directly, thanks to several data packages, for instance scRNAseq or HCAData.







NoteQuestion



Check out the He et al., Genome Biol. 2020 paper. Can you find a way to load the scRNAseq data from this paper without having to leave the R console?







NoteAnswer





scRNAseq::surveyDatasets() lists all the datasets available from the scRNAseq package, and scRNAseq::searchDatasets() finds datasets matching some keywords. Each dataset can then be fetched with fetchDataset().

})

title: 7  Lab 4 - Single-cell RNA-seq data wrangling
text:
7.1 Introduction
Data produced in a single cell RNA-seq experiment has several interesting characteristics that make it distinct from data produced in a bulk population RNA-seq experiment.
Two characteristics that are important to keep in mind when working with scRNA-Seq are drop-out (the excessive amount of zeros due to limiting mRNA) and the potential for quality control (QC) metrics to be confounded with biology. This combined with the ability to measure heterogeniety from cells in samples has shifted the field away from the typical analysis in population-based RNA-Seq.
Here we demonstrate some approaches to quality control, followed by identifying and analyzing cell subsets.

7.1.2 Create a SingleCellExperiment object from scratch
In the previous lab, we have been working with airway object (a SummarizedExperiment object) and sce, a SingleCellExperiment object. We will now create a toy SingleCellExperiment object from scratch, using the SingleCellExperiment constructor.
To create a SingleCellExperiment object, we need to provide the following:


colData: a data frame (or tibble) with columns corresponding to cell metadata.

rowData: a data frame (or tibble) with columns corresponding to gene metadata.

assays: a list of matrices, each matrix corresponding to a different assay. The first matrix is typically the counts matrix.

7.1.3 Read in kidney organoid counts matrix
We will now analyze a real human scRNAseq dataset, generated from iPSC-derived kidney organoids (Combes et al., Genome Medicine 2019). It is freely available from GEO: link. We start by downloading the cell, features and counts matrix of the fourth organoid (org4).







NoteQuestion

NoteAnswer





The links are listed in the “Supplementary file” box at the bottom of the GEO page. We use BiocFileCache (see Lab 3) to download them once, and get the path of their local copy:

title: 7  Lab 4 - Single-cell RNA-seq data wrangling
text:
7.2 Basic QCs
You can learn a lot about your scRNA-seq data’s quality with simple plotting. Let’s do some plotting to look at the number of reads per cell, reads per genes, expressed genes per cell (often called complexity), and rarity of genes (cells expressing genes).







NoteQuestion



Plot the number of counts per cell, the number of expressed genes per cell, and the relationship between the two.







NoteAnswer








R

counts_per_cell <- Matrix::colSums(counts)
counts_per_gene <- Matrix::rowSums(counts)
genes_per_cell <- Matrix::colSums(counts > 0) # count gene only if it has non-zero reads mapped.
hist(log10(counts_per_cell+1), main = '# of counts per cell', col = 'wheat')







hist(log10(genes_per_cell+1), main = '# of expressed genes per cell', col = 'wheat')






plot(counts_per_cell, genes_per_cell, log = 'xy', col = 'wheat')
title('Counts vs genes per cell')





















NoteQuestion



Look at the summary counts for genes and cells. Can you plot a histogram of counts per gene in log10 scale?







NoteAnswer








R

cells_per_gene <- Matrix::rowSums(counts > 0) # only count cells where the gene is expressed
hist(log10(cells_per_gene+1), main = '# of cells expressing each gene', col = 'wheat')















A very useful plot is the distribution of library complexity in the sequencing run, typically shown as a lineplot of the number of detected UMI per cell, with cells ranked in decreasing order. One can use such plot to investigate observations (potential cells) that are actually failed libraries (lower end outliers) or observations that are cell doublets (higher end outliers).







NoteQuestion



Plot cells ranked by their number of detected genes. Comment.







NoteAnswer








R

plot(
    sort(genes_per_cell, decreasing = TRUE),
    xlab = 'cell', log = 'y', main = '# of genes per cell (ordered)',
    type = 'l'
)















Several QCs can be automatically computed using quickRnaQc.se() from the scrapper package. scrapper provides fast C++ implementations of most steps of a scRNA-seq analysis (QC, normalization, variance modelling, PCA, clustering, marker detection…).






Notescuttle and scran are being replaced by scrapper



In previous Bioconductor releases, quality control metrics were computed with scuttle::quickPerCellQC() or scuttle::addPerCellQCMetrics(). Since Bioconductor 3.24, these functions (and most of scuttle and scran) are deprecated in favour of scrapper. You will still find them in many tutorials and in the OSCA book.


quickRnaQc.se() computes, for each cell, the total number of counts (sum), the number of detected genes (detected) and the proportion of counts assigned to any subsets of genes (e.g. mitochondrial genes). It then suggests filtering thresholds (cells with too few counts or detected genes, or with a too high proportion of mitochondrial counts, compared to the bulk of cells), and adds a keep column to the colData().



R

toy_sce <- scrapper::quickRnaQc.se(toy_sce, subsets = list())
colData(toy_sce)
##  DataFrame with 100 rows and 4 columns
##              idx       sum  detected      keep
##      <character> <numeric> <integer> <logical>

7.3 Access to stored informations

7.3.1 Assay slots
For typical scRNA-seq experiments, a SingleCellExperiment can have multiple assays, corresponding to different metrics. The most basic one is counts. Different assays store different ‘transformations’ of the counts (e.g. logcounts).
For example, one can compute mean-centered counts and store it in a new slot.



R

mean_centered_counts <- scale(counts(toy_sce), center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
assay(toy_sce, 'mean_centered') <- mean_centered_counts
assays(toy_sce)
##  List of length 2
##  names(2): counts mean_centered
assay(toy_sce, 'mean_centered')[1:10, 1:10]

Note that this is a very crude transformation, which does not account for differences in sequencing depth between cells: we will see in the next lectures and labs how to properly normalize counts (e.g. with scrapper::normalizeRnaCounts.se()).








7.3.2 Embeddings
Embeddings allow for a representation of large-scale data (N cells x M genes) into smaller dimensions (e.g. 2-50 dimensions). Typical embeddings can be PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, etc… Many embeddings can be computed using run...() functions from Bioconductor packages (e.g. scater, scrapper, …).
For example, one can compute PCA and store it in a new slot.



R

library(scater)
##  Loading required package: scuttle

logcounts(toy_sce) <- log10(counts(toy_sce) + 1)
toy_sce <- scater::runPCA(toy_sce, ncomponents = 2)
reducedDims(toy_sce)
##  List of length 1
##  names(1): PCA
reducedDim(toy_sce, 'PCA')[1:10, ]

##  [10,] -0.34225994  0.02170625
plotReducedDim(toy_sce, 'PCA')

Try to compute PCA, t-SNE and UMAP embeddings of the kidney organoid dataset using runPCA(), runTSNE() and runUMAP() from scater package.







NoteAnswer








R

sce <- scater::runPCA(sce)
plotReducedDim(sce, "PCA")








sce <- scater::runTSNE(sce)
plotReducedDim(sce, "TSNE")

plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP", colour_by = 'sum')






plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP", colour_by = 'detected')

7.4 Filtering cells and features

7.4.1 Pre-filtering
Filtering operations are often performed on the SingleCellExperiment object, for example to remove low-quality cells (columns) or genes (rows).
To do this, one can use standard R syntax to subset the SingleCellExperiment object.



R

toy_sce_filtered <- toy_sce[rowData(toy_sce)$gene_type == 'protein_coding', toy_sce$sum > 50]
toy_sce_filtered
##  class: SingleCellExperiment 
##  dim: 5 44 
##  metadata(1): qc
##  assays(3): counts mean_centered logcounts
##  rownames: NULL
##  rowData names(2): gene_name gene_type
##  colnames: NULL
##  colData names(4): idx sum detected keep
##  reducedDimNames(1): PCA
##  mainExpName: NULL
##  altExpNames(0):









NoteQuestion



Filter the SCE to only include cells that have a complexity of 2000 genes or more and genes that are are expressed in 10 or more cells.







NoteAnswer








R

sce_filtered <- sce[
    Matrix::rowSums(counts(sce) > 0) >= 10,
    Matrix::colSums(counts(sce) > 0) >= 2000
]
sce_filtered
##  class: SingleCellExperiment 
##  dim: 16820 1419 
##  metadata(1): qc
##  assays(2): counts logcounts
##  rownames(16820): ENSG00000279457 ENSG00000228463 ... ENSG00000276345
##    ENSG00000271254
##  rowData names(2): X1 X2
##  colnames(1419): AAACCTGAGGCTCATT-1 AAACCTGAGGTGCACA-1 ...
##    TTTGTCAGTCTCACCT-1 TTTGTCAGTGAAATCA-1
##  colData names(5): X1 sum detected subset.proportion.mito keep
##  reducedDimNames(3): PCA TSNE UMAP
##  mainExpName: NULL
##  altExpNames(0):









Almost all our analysis will be on this single object, of class SingleCellExperiment. This object contains various “slots” that will store not only the raw count data, but also the results from various computations below. This has the advantage that we do not need to keep track of inidividual variables of interest - they can all be collapsed into a single object as long as these slots are pre-defined.

7.4.2 Filtering low-quality cells: mitochondrial counts
For each cell, we can calculate the percentage of counts mapping on mitochondrial genes and store it in a column percent_mito in our colData().



R

rowData(sce_filtered)
##  DataFrame with 16820 rows and 2 columns
##                               X1            X2
##                      <character>   <character>
##  ENSG00000279457 ENSG00000279457    FO538757.2
##  ENSG00000228463 ENSG00000228463    AP006222.2
##  ENSG00000237094 ENSG00000237094 RP4-669L17.10
##  ENSG00000237491 ENSG00000237491 RP11-206L10.9
##  ENSG00000225880 ENSG00000225880     LINC00115
##  ...                         ...           ...
##  ENSG00000276256 ENSG00000276256    AC011043.1
##  ENSG00000273748 ENSG00000273748    AL592183.1
##  ENSG00000278817 ENSG00000278817    AC007325.4
##  ENSG00000276345 ENSG00000276345    AC004556.1
##  ENSG00000271254 ENSG00000271254    AC240274.1
mito_genes <- rownames(sce_filtered)[grep(pattern = "^MT-", x = rowData(sce_filtered)$X2)]
mito_genes
##   [1] "ENSG00000198888" "ENSG00000198763" "ENSG00000198804" "ENSG00000198712"
##   [5] "ENSG00000228253" "ENSG00000198899" "ENSG00000198938" "ENSG00000198840"
##   [9] "ENSG00000212907" "ENSG00000198886" "ENSG00000198786" "ENSG00000198695"
##  [13] "ENSG00000198727"
mito_genes_counts <- counts(sce_filtered)[mito_genes, ]
percent_mito <- Matrix::colSums(mito_genes_counts) / sce_filtered$sum
hist(percent_mito*100, main = '% of total counts over mitochondrial genes', col = 'wheat')







colData(sce_filtered)$percent_mito <- percent_mito
table(colData(sce_filtered)$percent_mito > 0.1)
##  
##  FALSE  TRUE 
##   1398    21








NoteQuestion



Remove cells with a % of mitochondrial counts greater than 10%.







NoteAnswer








R

sce_filtered <- sce_filtered[
    ,
    sce_filtered$percent_mito <= 0.10
]
sce_filtered

##  dim: 16820 1398 
##  metadata(1): qc
##  assays(2): counts logcounts

##  reducedDimNames(3): PCA TSNE UMAP
##  mainExpName: NULL
##  altExpNames(0):










7.4.3 Checking housekeeping genes
Another metric we use is the number of house keeping genes expressed in a cell. These genes reflect commomn processes active in a cell and hence are a good global quality measure. They are also abundant and are usually steadliy expressed in cells, thus less sensitive to the high dropout.
We first load the list of housekeeping genes curated by Tirosh et al., Science 2016 (shipped with this book), match them to the genes in the rowData of the SingleCellExperiment object (using match and rownames), remove NAs (genes not found in the rowData), and store the list of housekeeping genes in a new variable.



R

# Load the list of housekeeping genes
hk_file <- system.file("extdata", "tirosh_house_keeping.txt", package = "scRNAseqPhysalia2026")
hkgenes <- read.table(hk_file, skip = 2)
hkgenes <- as.vector(hkgenes$V1)
hkgenes <- rownames(sce_filtered)[match(hkgenes, rowData(sce_filtered)$X2)]
hkgenes <- hkgenes[!is.na(hkgenes)]
hkgenes

7.4.4 Checking gene set expression
Sometimes we want to ask what is the expression of a gene / a set of a genes across cells. This set of genes may make up a gene expression program we are interested in. Another benefit at looking at gene sets is it reduces the effects of drop outs.
Let’s look at genes involved in the stress signature upon cell dissociation. We calculate these genes average expression levels on the single cell level.



R

genes_dissoc <- c("ATF3", "BTG2", "CEBPB", "CEBPD", "CXCL3", "CXCL2", "CXCL1", "DNAJA1", "DNAJB1", "DUSP1", "EGR1", "FOS", "FOSB", "HSP90AA1", "HSP90AB1", "HSPA1A", "HSPA1B", "HSPA1A", "HSPA1B", "HSPA8", "HSPB1", "HSPE1", "HSPH1", "ID3", "IER2", "JUN", "JUNB", "JUND", "MT1X", "NFKBIA", "NR4A1", "PPP1R15A", "SOCS3", "ZFP36")
genes_dissoc <- rownames(sce_filtered)[match(genes_dissoc, rowData(sce_filtered)$X2)]
genes_dissoc <- unique(genes_dissoc[!is.na(genes_dissoc)])









NoteQuestion



Calculate the average gene set expression for each cell.







NoteAnswer








R

ave_expr_genes_dissoc <- Matrix::colMeans(logcounts(sce_filtered[genes_dissoc, ]))
colData(sce_filtered)$ave_expr_genes_dissoc <- ave_expr_genes_dissoc
















NoteQuestion

NoteAnswer








R

plotReducedDim(sce_filtered, dimred = 'PCA', colour_by = 'ave_expr_genes_dissoc')







plotReducedDim(sce_filtered, dimred = 'UMAP', colour_by = 'ave_expr_genes_dissoc')

9.1.1 Preparing dataset
We will prepare scRNAseq data from a PBMC run, provided by 10X and hosted by Bioconductor as a package.







NoteQuestion



Which package from Bioconductor gives streamlined access to PBMC scRNAseq dataset from 10X Genomics?
What does the object contain (type of data, number of cells, batches, organism, …)? Can you get the same data from somewhere else?

R

library(tidyverse)

9.1.2 Normalize counts using scran

Just like in bulk high-throughput sequencing experiments, scRNAseq counts have to be normalized to the sequencing depth for each cell. We can define the library size as the total sum of counts across all genes for each cell, the expected value of which is assumed to scale with any cell-specific biases. However, this relies on the assumption that within the entire dataset, most genes are non-differentially expressed and expressed roughly within the same range. Depending on the set up of the scRNAseq experiment, this can be entirely false. To avoid relying on this hypothesis, we can (1) quickly pre-cluster cells, then (2) normalize cells using their library size factor separately in each cluster, then (3) rescaling size factors so that they are comparable across clusters.
All of this can be done very simply using the combo quickCluster() + computeSumFactors() from the scran package, followed by normalizeRnaCounts.se() from the scrapper package.

normalizeRnaCounts.se() divides the counts of each cell by its size factor, then log-transforms them (log2(x + 1)). Note that the logcounts assay is not a regular matrix: it is a LogNormalizedMatrix, which only stores the counts and the size factors, and computes the log-normalized values on the fly. This saves a lot of memory for large datasets!








9.1.3 Feature selection
We often use scRNAseq data in exploratory analyses to characterize heterogeneity across cells. Procedures like clustering and dimensionality reduction compare cells based on their gene expression profiles. The choice of genes to include in this comparison may have a major impact on the performance of downstream methods. Ideally, one wants to only select genes that contain useful information about the biology of the system while removing genes that contain random noise. This aims to preserve interesting biological structure without the variance that obscures that structure.
The simplest approach to feature selection is to compute the variance of the log-normalized expression values, to select the most variable genes. Modelling of the mean-variance relationship can be achieved by the modelGeneVariances() function from the scrapper package: it computes the mean and the variance of the log-normalized expression of each gene, fits a trend to the variance with respect to the mean (the technical variance), and computes the residual from this trend for each gene (the biological variance).

9.1.4 PCA on filtered dataset
We now have normalized counts filtered for the top 10% genes varying with the greatest biological significance. Still, that represents a ~3,400 x nCells (~4,300) dataset (each row being a feature). This is still too big to reliably use in standard clustering approaches. We can further compress the dataset. The most widely used approach is PCA: it computes a small number of “components” (typically 5-50) optimally summarizing the variability of the whole dataset, while retaining linearity of the underlying numerical data and being computationallt quite efficient.







NoteQuestion



Use the runPca.se() function from the scrapper package to compute a PCA embedding of the data, using the highly variable genes only.
How much of the variance is explained by each principal component? How many components would you keep for downstream analyses?







NoteAnswer








R

set.seed(1000)
sce <- scrapper::runPca.se(sce, features = rowData(sce)$isHVG, number = 50)
reducedDim(sce, 'PCA')[1:5, 1:5]

##  [1,] 16.874448 0.8689463 -1.0040325 4.6334941  1.75547776

##  [4,] -6.381954 2.8499857  0.3208111 0.2344315  3.75205924
##  [5,] -8.227185 1.5069442 -5.0113033 1.6077754  0.83386219

plot(percent_var, xlab = 'PC', ylab = 'Variance explained (%)', type = 'b')








The “elbow” of this curve suggests that the first ~15 PCs capture most of the biological signal, and that the next ones mostly capture noise. We keep the first 15 PCs for downstream analyses:

9.2 Clustering
Clustering is an unsupervised learning procedure that is used in scRNA-seq data analysis to empirically define groups of cells with similar expression profiles. Its primary purpose is to summarize the data in a digestible format for human interpretation.
After annotation based on marker genes, the clusters can be treated as proxies for more abstract biological concepts such as cell types or states. Clustering is thus a critical step for extracting biological insights from scRNA-seq data.

9.2.1 Clustering algorithms
Three main approaches can be used:

Hierarchical clustering
k-means clustering
Graph-based clustering

Today, we will focus on graph-based clustering, as it is becoming the standard for scRNAseq: it is a flexible and scalable technique for clustering even the largest scRNA-seq datasets. We first build a graph where each node is a cell that is connected by edges to its nearest neighbors in the high-dimensional space. Edges are weighted based on the similarity between the cells involved, with higher weight given to cells that are more closely related.







NoteQuestion



Compute a graph-based clustering of the PBMC dataset.







NoteAnswer








R

set.seed(1000)
graph <- bluster::makeSNNGraph(reducedDim(sce, 'PCA'), k = 5)

9.2.2 Dimensional reduction for clustering visualization
PCA is a powerful linear approach to compress large datasets into smaller dimensional spaces. However, it struggles at emphasizing the existence of clusters in complex datasets, when visualized in 2D.

UMAP
Diffusion Map
Multi-Dimensional Scaling (MDS)
Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF)

9.3 Cell annotation

9.3.1 Find marker genes
To interpret clustering results, one needs to identify the genes that drive separation between clusters. These marker genes allow to assign biological meaning to each cluster based on their functional annotation. In the most obvious case, the marker genes for each cluster are a priori associated with particular cell types, allowing us to treat the clustering as a proxy for cell type identity.
A general strategy is to compare each cluster to each of the other clusters, gene by gene, and then to combine the results of all these pairwise comparisons into a single ranking of marker genes for each cluster.
Rather than p-values (which are not really meaningful here: the clusters were defined from the very same data!), scrapper::scoreMarkers.se() computes several effect sizes for each pairwise comparison:


cohens.d: the difference in mean log-expression, divided by the standard deviation;

auc: the probability that a random cell from the cluster has a higher expression than a random cell from the other cluster;

delta.mean: the difference in mean log-expression (i.e. a log-fold change);

delta.detected: the difference in the proportion of cells in which the gene is detected.

For each gene and each cluster, these effect sizes are then summarized across all the pairwise comparisons (min, mean, median, max, min.rank).

markers <- scrapper::scoreMarkers.se(sce, groups = sce$clusters_graph)

11.2 Harmonize the four datasets
Datasets published by different labs rarely look alike: genes may be named differently, cell annotations may be stored in different columns (with different names for the same cell types), counts may not be integers… Before anything else, we need to make the four datasets consistent.







NoteQuestion




How are genes named in each dataset? Use gene symbols for all of them.
Which cell annotations are available? Gather them in a common celltype column.








NoteAnswer








R

head(rownames(celseq))
##  [1] "A1BG-AS1__chr19" "A1BG__chr19"     "A1CF__chr10"     "A2M-AS1__chr12" 
##  [5] "A2ML1__chr12"    "A2MP1__chr12"
head(rownames(celseq2))
##  [1] "A1BG-AS1__chr19" "A1BG__chr19"     "A1CF__chr10"     "A2M-AS1__chr12" 
##  [5] "A2ML1__chr12"    "A2M__chr12"
head(rownames(fluidigmc1))
##  [1] "ENSG00000229483" "ENSG00000232849" "ENSG00000229558" "ENSG00000232977"
##  [5] "ENSG00000227893" "ENSG00000238230"
head(rownames(smartseq2))
##  [1] "SGIP1"   "AZIN2"   "CLIC4"   "AGBL4"   "NECAP2"  "SLC45A1"


CEL-seq and CEL-seq2 datasets store gene symbols in their rowData, and the Fluidigm C1 dataset uses Ensembl gene IDs, which we can translate into gene symbols with the org.Hs.eg.db annotation package.



R

rownames(celseq) <- rowData(celseq)$symbol
rownames(celseq2) <- rowData(celseq2)$symbol
rownames(fluidigmc1) <- AnnotationDbi::mapIds(
    org.Hs.eg.db::org.Hs.eg.db, keys = rownames(fluidigmc1),
    keytype = "ENSEMBL", column = "SYMBOL"
)
##  
##  'select()' returned 1:many mapping between keys and columns

## - Remove genes without a symbol, or with a duplicated symbol
clean_genes <- function(sce) {
    sce[!is.na(rownames(sce)) & !duplicated(rownames(sce)), ]
}
celseq <- clean_genes(celseq)
celseq2 <- clean_genes(celseq2)
fluidigmc1 <- clean_genes(fluidigmc1)
smartseq2 <- clean_genes(smartseq2)


Cell annotations are found in the label (CEL-seq2), cell type (Fluidigm C1) and inferred cell type (Smart-seq2) columns. The CEL-seq dataset does not come with cell annotations.



R

harmonize_labels <- function(x) {
    x <- sub(" cell$", "", tolower(x))
    dplyr::case_when(
        x %in% c("alpha", "beta", "delta", "acinar") ~ x,
        x %in% c("gamma", "pp", "gamma/pp") ~ "gamma/PP",
        x %in% c("duct", "ductal") ~ "ductal",
        is.na(x) ~ NA_character_,
        TRUE ~ "other"
    )
}
celseq$celltype <- NA_character_
celseq2$celltype <- harmonize_labels(celseq2$label)
fluidigmc1$celltype <- harmonize_labels(fluidigmc1$`cell type`)
smartseq2$celltype <- harmonize_labels(smartseq2$`inferred cell type`)

Finally, we keep a minimal and consistent set of information for each dataset: the counts (rounded to integers and stored as sparse matrices), the cell type and the technology.

    SingleCellExperiment(

11.3 Analyze each pancreas dataset without batch correction
We will first analyze each dataset separately to see if there are any differences between the datasets.







NoteQuestion



What is the size of each single cell RNA-seq dataset?
Briefly describe the technology used to collect each dataset.
Which datasets do you expect to be different and which do you expect to be similar?







NoteAnswer








R

dim(celseq)

dim(celseq2)
##  [1] 19046  3072

NoteQuestion



Compute QC metrics for each dataset, and look at the distributions of number of genes per cell.







NoteAnswer








R

library(ggplot2)

celseq_raw <- scrapper::quickRnaQc.se(celseq, subsets = list())

    data.frame(tech = celseq_raw$tech, nGenes = celseq_raw$detected, totalUMIs = celseq_raw$sum),
    data.frame(tech = celseq2_raw$tech, nGenes = celseq2_raw$detected, totalUMIs = celseq2_raw$sum),
    data.frame(tech = fluidigmc1_raw$tech, nGenes = fluidigmc1_raw$detected, totalUMIs = fluidigmc1_raw$sum),
    data.frame(tech = smartseq2_raw$tech, nGenes = smartseq2_raw$detected, totalUMIs = smartseq2_raw$sum)

    geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, position = position_dodge(0.9), outlier.shape = NA) +
    theme_minimal() +
    ylab("Number of genes detected per cell") +
    xlab("Technology")

    geom_violin(trim = TRUE) +
    geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, position = position_dodge(0.9), outlier.shape = NA) +
    theme_minimal() +
    ylab("Total number of UMIs (or reads) detected per cell (log10)") +
    xlab("Technology")














Now we will subset the data to remove cells with low gene counts.







NoteQuestion



Subset the data to remove cells with:

fewer than 1750 genes for CEL-Seq;
fewer than 2500 genes for CEL-Seq2;
fewer than 2500 genes for SMART-Seq2.








NoteAnswer








R

celseq <- celseq_raw[ , celseq_raw$detected > 1750 ]
celseq2 <- celseq2_raw[ , celseq2_raw$detected > 2500 ]
smartseq2 <- smartseq2_raw[ , smartseq2_raw$detected > 2500 ]
fluidigmc1 <- fluidigmc1_raw
c(celseq = ncol(celseq), celseq2 = ncol(celseq2), fluidigmc1 = ncol(fluidigmc1), smartseq2 = ncol(smartseq2))
##      celseq    celseq2 fluidigmc1  smartseq2 
##         998       2283        638       2394









Now we will subsample each dataset to only have 500 cells. This is to speed up subsequent analyses. Often when we are setting up our analysis, we work with a subset of the data to make iteration across analysis decisions faster, and once we have finalized how we want to do the analysis, we work with the full dataset.







NoteQuestion



Randomly subsample each full dataset to 500 cells.







NoteAnswer








R

set.seed(42)
celseq <- celseq[ , sample(colnames(celseq), 500) ]
celseq2 <- celseq2[ , sample(colnames(celseq2), 500) ]
fluidigmc1 <- fluidigmc1[ , sample(colnames(fluidigmc1), 500) ]
smartseq2 <- smartseq2[ , sample(colnames(smartseq2), 500) ]









Now we will subset each dataset to only retain the common genes across all four datasets.







NoteQuestion




Using Reduce, find the common genes across all four datasets.
Subset each dataset to only retain these common genes.








NoteAnswer








R

common_genes <- Reduce(intersect, list(
    rownames(celseq),
    rownames(celseq2),
    rownames(fluidigmc1),
    rownames(smartseq2)
))
length(common_genes)
##  [1] 14958

celseq <- celseq[common_genes, ]
celseq2 <- celseq2[common_genes, ]
fluidigmc1 <- fluidigmc1[common_genes, ]
smartseq2 <- smartseq2[common_genes, ]

title: 11  Lab 6: Batch correction
text:
11.4 Individual processing
Like what we have done in previous labs, we will now normalize, identify variable genes, and perform PCA embedding. Note that we ask normalizeRnaCounts.se() to store the log-normalized counts as an actual sparse matrix (delayed = FALSE) rather than as a LogNormalizedMatrix: some tools, such as batchelor, are much faster with it.



R

process_batch <- function(sce) {
    clusters <- scran::quickCluster(sce)
    sce <- scran::computeSumFactors(sce, clusters = clusters)
    sce <- scrapper::normalizeRnaCounts.se(
        sce, size.factors = sizeFactors(sce), more.norm.args = list(delayed = FALSE)
    )
    sce <- scrapper::chooseRnaHvgs.se(sce, top = 2000)
    sce <- scrapper::runPca.se(sce, features = rowData(sce)$hvg, number = 50)
    return(sce)
}
set.seed(42)
celseq <- process_batch(celseq)
celseq2 <- process_batch(celseq2)
fluidigmc1 <- process_batch(fluidigmc1)
smartseq2 <- process_batch(smartseq2)


The integration workflows require the identification of shared variable genes. Why would we need such a requirement?







NoteQuestion



Find the genes which are highly variable in all four datasets.







NoteAnswer








R

shared_hvgs <- Reduce(intersect, list(
    rownames(celseq)[rowData(celseq)$hvg],
    rownames(celseq2)[rowData(celseq2)$hvg],
    rownames(fluidigmc1)[rowData(fluidigmc1)$hvg],
    rownames(smartseq2)[rowData(smartseq2)$hvg]
))

length(shared_hvgs)
##  [1] 377

title: 11  Lab 6: Batch correction
text:
11.5 Without batch correction
Let’s first merge the four datasets and analyze them together, without any batch correction.







NoteQuestion




Merge the four datasets in a single SingleCellExperiment object.
Compute a PCA and a UMAP embedding of the merged data, using the shared highly variable genes.
Plot the UMAP embedding, coloring cells by technology and by cell type. Comment.








NoteAnswer








R

library(scater)
##  Loading required package: scuttle
library(patchwork)
batches <- list(celseq = celseq, celseq2 = celseq2, fluidigmc1 = fluidigmc1, smartseq2 = smartseq2)
merged <- SingleCellExperiment(
    assays = list(
        counts = do.call(cbind, lapply(batches, counts)),
        logcounts = do.call(cbind, lapply(batches, logcounts))
    ),
    colData = do.call(rbind, lapply(batches, function(x) colData(x)[, c("celltype", "tech")]))
)
merged
##  class: SingleCellExperiment 
##  dim: 14958 2000 
##  metadata(0):
##  assays(2): counts logcounts
##  rownames(14958): A1BG A1CF ... ZZEF1 ZZZ3
##  rowData names(0):
##  colnames(2000): D102_50 D17TGFB_94 ... HP1502401_C12 HP1525301T2D_O2
##  colData names(2): celltype tech
##  reducedDimNames(0):
##  mainExpName: NULL
##  altExpNames(0):
set.seed(42)
merged <- scrapper::runPca.se(merged, features = rownames(merged) %in% shared_hvgs, number = 50)
merged <- runUMAP(merged, dimred = "PCA", n_neighbors = 15, min_dist = 0.5)
plotUMAP(merged, colour_by = "tech") + ggtitle("Uncorrected: technology") +
    plotUMAP(merged, colour_by = "celltype") + ggtitle("Uncorrected: cell type")

title: 11  Lab 6: Batch correction
text:
11.6 Batch correction with MNN
We will now use MNN to see to what extent it can remove potential batch effects.







NoteQuestion




Use the fastMNN function to perform MNN batch correction across the four datasets.








NoteAnswer








R

library(batchelor)

set.seed(42)
merged_mnn <- fastMNN(
    celseq = celseq,
    celseq2 = celseq2,
    fluidigmc1 = fluidigmc1,
    smartseq2 = smartseq2,
    subset.row = shared_hvgs,
    d = 50,
    correct.all = TRUE
)

Let’s look at how well the batches have mixed after MNN correction.
