title: 11  Lab 6: Batch correction
text:
11.7 Batch correction with Harmony
Harmony is another widely used method, which iteratively clusters cells in the PCA space and corrects the cluster centroids of each batch towards the global centroids. It is very fast, and also works directly on the PCA embedding.







NoteQuestion



Use harmony::RunHarmony() to correct the PCA embedding of the merged (uncorrected) data, then plot a UMAP embedding of the corrected data. Compare it to the MNN results.







NoteAnswer








R

set.seed(42)
merged <- harmony::RunHarmony(merged, group.by.vars = "tech")
##  Transposing data matrix
##  Using automatic lambda estimation
##  Thetas: 2
##  Initializing state using k-means centroids initialization
##  Initializing centroids
##  Harmony 1/10
##  Harmony 2/10
##  Harmony 3/10
##  Harmony 4/10
##  Harmony 5/10
##  Harmony converged after 5 iterations
reducedDimNames(merged)
##  [1] "PCA"     "UMAP"    "HARMONY"
merged <- runUMAP(merged, dimred = "HARMONY", n_neighbors = 15, min_dist = 0.5, name = "UMAP_HARMONY")
plotReducedDim(merged, "UMAP_HARMONY", colour_by = "tech") + ggtitle("Harmony: technology") +
    plotReducedDim(merged, "UMAP_HARMONY", colour_by = "celltype") + ggtitle("Harmony: cell type")

title: 11  Lab 6: Batch correction
section: 11.8 Batch correction: integrative non-negative matrix factorization (NMF)
text:
11.8 Batch correction: integrative non-negative matrix factorization (NMF)
Here we use integrative non-negative matrix factorization (NMF/LIGER) to see to what extent it can remove potential batch effects.
The important parameters in the batch correction are the number of factors (k), the penalty parameter (lambda), and the clustering resolution. The number of factors sets the number of factors (consisting of shared and dataset-specific factors) used in factorizing the matrix. The penalty parameter sets the balance between factors shared across the batches and factors specific to the individual batches. The default setting of lambda=5.0 is usually used by the Macosko lab. Resolution=1.0 is used in the Louvain clustering of the shared neighbor factors that have been quantile normalized.



R

ob.list <- list(
    "celseq" = counts(celseq),
    "celseq2" = counts(celseq2),
    "fluidigmc1" = counts(fluidigmc1),
    "smartseq2" = counts(smartseq2)
)

# Create a LIGER object with raw counts data from each batch.
library(rliger)
##  Package `rliger` has been updated massively since version 1.99.0, including the object structure which is not compatible with old versions.
##  
##  We recommand you backup your old analysis before overwriting any existing result.
##  
##  `readLiger()` is provided for reading an RDS file storing an old object and it converts the object to the up-to-date structure.
##  
##  Attaching package: 'rliger'
##  The following objects are masked from 'package:scater':
##  
##      normalize, runTSNE, runUMAP
##  The following object is masked from 'package:BiocGenerics':
##  
##      normalize
options(ligerVerbose = FALSE)
data.liger <- createLiger(ob.list)
##  ! No human mitochondrial gene found in the union of dataset "celseq"
##  ℹ Updated QC variables: "nUMI", "nGene", "mito", "ribo", and "hemo"
##  ! No human mitochondrial gene found in the union of dataset "celseq2"
##  ℹ Updated QC variables: "nUMI", "nGene", "mito", "ribo", and "hemo"
##  ! No human mitochondrial gene found in the union of dataset "fluidigmc1"
##  ℹ Updated QC variables: "nUMI", "nGene", "mito", "ribo", and "hemo"
##  ! No human mitochondrial gene found in the union of dataset "smartseq2"
##  ℹ Updated QC variables: "nUMI", "nGene", "mito", "ribo", and "hemo"

# Normalize gene expression for each batch.
data.liger <- rliger::normalize(data.liger)

# Find variable genes for LIGER analysis. Identify variable genes that are variable across most samples.
data.liger <- selectGenes(data.liger)









NoteQuestion



Scale the gene expression across the datasets.







NoteAnswer








R

data.liger <- scaleNotCenter(data.liger)









Next, we will run the integrative non-negative matrix factorization.







NoteQuestion



Use the runIntegration function to perform the integrative non-negative matrix factorization.







NoteAnswer








R

data.liger <- runIntegration(data.liger, k = 30)






What do matrices H, V, and W represent, and what are their dimensions?







NoteAnswer








R

dim(getMatrix(data.liger, "H")$celseq)
##  [1]  30 500
dim(getMatrix(data.liger, "V")$celseq)
##  [1] 14605    30
dim(getMatrix(data.liger, "W"))
##  [1] 14605    30









Next, do normalization and clustering of cells in shared nearest factor space.







NoteQuestion



Do quantile normalization, cluster quantile normalized data







NoteAnswer








R

data.liger <- quantileNorm(data.liger)
##  ℹ Using largest dataset of recommended type as reference: "celseq" with 500 cells
data.liger <- runCluster(data.liger, resolution = 1)






What are the dimensions of H.norm. What does this represent?







NoteAnswer








R

dim(getMatrix(data.liger, "H.norm"))
##  [1] 2000   30









Let’s see what the liger data looks like mapped onto a UMAP visualization.







NoteQuestion



Run UMAP on the quantile normalized data and visualize the clusters.







NoteAnswer








R

merged_liger <- SingleCellExperiment(
    colData = cellMeta(data.liger),
    reducedDims = list(liger = getMatrix(data.liger, "H.norm"))
)
merged_liger$celltype <- merged$celltype[match(merged_liger$barcode, colnames(merged))]
set.seed(42)
## `rliger` also provides a `runUMAP()` function: we explicitly use the one from `scater`
merged_liger <- scater::runUMAP(merged_liger, dimred = 'liger', n_neighbors = 15, min_dist = 0.5)
plotUMAP(merged_liger, colour_by = "dataset") + ggtitle("LIGER: technology") +
    plotUMAP(merged_liger, colour_by = "celltype") + ggtitle("LIGER: cell type")

title: 11  Lab 6: Batch correction
text:
11.9 Clustering and differential gene expression
Clustering can now be performed over the integrated data (using merged_mnn here). Here we use the Louvain clustering algorithm.
Then, differential gene expression is performed between clusters, using a pseudobulk approach: counts are summed across all cells of each cluster, in each batch. Note that we use the original count data in all DE tests. We should never use values from the integrated data in DE tests, as they violate assumptions of independence among samples that are required for DE tests!







NoteQuestion




Perform clustering on the MNN integrated data.








NoteAnswer








R

merged_mnn <- scrapper::clusterGraph.se(merged_mnn, reddim.type = "corrected", output.name = "cluster")
merged_mnn$cluster <- factor(merged_mnn$cluster)

table(merged_mnn$cluster, merged_mnn$batch)
##     
##      celseq celseq2 fluidigmc1 smartseq2
##    1     27      42         19        27
##    2     77     152         99       111
##    3    137      53         24        79
##    4    140      58         18        34
##    5     82     102        202        70
##    6     13      24         16        52
##    7     14      32         20        21
##    8     10      37        102       106
table(merged_mnn$cluster, merged_mnn$celltype)
##     
##      acinar alpha beta delta ductal gamma/PP other
##    1      0     1    1    81      0        0     2
##    2      0   338    0     0      0        0     3
##    3      0     0    0     2    137        0     4
##    4     96     1    1     0      1        1     0
##    5      0     0  356     1      1        0     9
##    6      0     0    1     0      1       83     3
##    7      0     1    0     1      5        0    57
##    8      0   218    2     0      1        0     9







Aggregate cells across batches and clusters to prepare pseudobulk data.








NoteAnswer








R

pseudobulk <- scrapper::aggregateAcrossCells.se(
    merged_mnn,
    factors = list(batch = merged_mnn$batch, cluster = merged_mnn$cluster),
    assay.type = "counts"
)
pseudobulk
##  class: RangedSummarizedExperiment 
##  dim: 14958 32 
##  metadata(1): aggregated
##  assays(2): sums detected
##  rownames(14958): A1BG A1CF ... ZZEF1 ZZZ3
##  rowData names(1): rotation
##  colnames: NULL
##  colData names(6): factor.batch factor.cluster ... celltype cluster
colData(pseudobulk)[, c("factor.batch", "factor.cluster", "counts")]
##  DataFrame with 32 rows and 3 columns
##      factor.batch factor.cluster    counts
##       <character>       <factor> <integer>
##  1         celseq              1        27
##  2         celseq              2        77
##  3         celseq              3       137
##  4         celseq              4       140
##  5         celseq              5        82
##  ...          ...            ...       ...
##  28     smartseq2              4        34
##  29     smartseq2              5        70
##  30     smartseq2              6        52
##  31     smartseq2              7        21
##  32     smartseq2              8       106

## - Only keep pseudo-samples aggregating at least 10 cells
pseudobulk <- pseudobulk[, pseudobulk$counts >= 10]
pseudobulk_se <- SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = assay(pseudobulk, "sums")),
    colData = DataFrame(
        batch = factor(pseudobulk$factor.batch),
        cluster = factor(pseudobulk$factor.cluster)
    )
)
pseudobulk_se
##  class: SummarizedExperiment 
##  dim: 14958 32 
##  metadata(0):
##  assays(1): counts
##  rownames(14958): A1BG A1CF ... ZZEF1 ZZZ3
##  rowData names(0):
##  colnames: NULL
##  colData names(2): batch cluster







Perform differential gene expression analysis across clusters.








NoteAnswer








R

library(DESeq2)
##  
##  Attaching package: 'DESeq2'
##  The following object is masked from 'package:scater':
##  
##      fpkm
dds <- DESeqDataSet(pseudobulk_se, design = ~ batch + cluster)
##  converting counts to integer mode
dds <- DESeq(dds)
##  estimating size factors
##  estimating dispersions
##  gene-wise dispersion estimates
##  mean-dispersion relationship
##  final dispersion estimates
##  fitting model and testing
resultsNames(dds)
##   [1] "Intercept"                  "batch_celseq2_vs_celseq"

res <- results(dds, contrast = c("cluster", levels(dds$cluster)[2], levels(dds$cluster)[1]))
res[order(res$padj), ]

title: 13  Lab 7: Single-cell ATAC-seq analysis workflow
text:
13.1 Process human PBMC dataset
ATAC-seq data may be obtained in isolation using a single-cell ATAC-seq protocol (e.g. 10X scATACseq) or in combination with gene expression data using a single-cell multiome protocole (e.g. 10X multiome and SHARE-seq).
Several packages are currently avaialble to process scATAC-seq data in R. These include Signac and ArchR. This lab will closely follow the processing steps outlined in Signac, which interfaces well with Seurat for single-cell analysis.
In this lab, we will process a PBMC single-cell ATAC-seq (scATAC-seq) dataset and perform preliminary analysis to assess quality of these data. The data for this lab comes from 10X Genomics. The dataset contains roughly ~ 10,000 cells.
crumbs: 13  Lab 7: Single-cell ATAC-seq analysis workflow

title: 13  Lab 7: Single-cell ATAC-seq analysis workflow
text:
13.1.1 Download data
The files we need are directly available from the 10x Genomics website. We download them in a ~/data/scATAC folder (this may take a few minutes, the fragments file weighs ~2 GB). Note that the fragments file and its index (.tbi) must sit next to each other, with matching names.



R

scatac_dir <- file.path(path.expand("~"), "data", "scATAC")
dir.create(scatac_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
options(timeout = 3600)
url <- "https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/cell-atac/1.0.1/atac_v1_pbmc_10k/"
files <- c(
    "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_filtered_peak_bc_matrix.h5", 
    "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_peaks.bed", 
    "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_singlecell.csv", 
    "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_fragments.tsv.gz", 
    "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_fragments.tsv.gz.tbi"
)
for (f in files) {
    if (!file.exists(file.path(scatac_dir, f))) 
        download.file(paste0(url, f), destfile = file.path(scatac_dir, f))
}
list.files(scatac_dir)
h5_file <- file.path(scatac_dir, "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_filtered_peak_bc_matrix.h5")
peaks_file <- file.path(scatac_dir, "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_peaks.bed")
metadata_file <- file.path(scatac_dir, "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_singlecell.csv")
fragments_file <- file.path(scatac_dir, "atac_v1_pbmc_10k_fragments.tsv.gz")



13.1.2 Import data
Notice how the count matrix is in a .h5 format. We have already encountered this kind of 10x Genomics outputs in Lab 3. Back then, we imported them with DropletUtils::read10xCounts.







NoteQuestion



Does this function work here?







NoteAnswer








R

scatac <- DropletUtils::read10xCounts(h5_file)
scatac









This works because 10X Genomics make sure to distribute files in .h5 format that are consistent accross single-cell sequencing methodologies.
However, the SingleCellExperiment obtained with this approach is not the most convenient, as it cannot natively leverage fragments file (see below).
Instead, we can create a Signac object, a flavour of Seurat objects.







NoteQuestion



Import counts matrix and feature annotations using an import function provided by Seurat.







NoteAnswer








R

library(Seurat)
library(Signac)
library(rtracklayer)
library(stringr)
cnts <- Read10X_h5(h5_file)
features <- import(peaks_file)
features$peak <- as.character(features) |> str_replace(':', '-')
metadata <- read.csv(
  file = metadata_file,
  header = TRUE,
  row.names = 1
)






How many accessible genomic segments were found in this dataset?







NoteAnswer








R

features
length(features)










13.1.3 Create a Seurat object
The next step is to aggregate counts and features into a ChromatinAssay, a scATAC-seq flavour of Seurat standard Assays. The documentation for ?CreateChromatinAssay indicates that the user can provide:

A fragments file, corresponding to the full list of all unique fragments mapped across all single cells.
Genomic annotations to the ChromatinAssay, corresponding to gene annotations, promoter positions, etc. Such annotations can be generated from Ensembl.








NoteQuestion



Generate human annotations from Ensembl using a parsing function from Signac.







NoteAnswer








R

## - Get human gene annotations (hg19/GRCh37) to feed it into the future `ChromatinAssay`
annotations <- GetGRangesFromEnsDb(ensdb = EnsDb.Hsapiens.v75::EnsDb.Hsapiens.v75)
GenomeInfoDb::seqlevelsStyle(annotations) <- 'UCSC'
GenomeInfoDb::genome(annotations) <- "hg19"






Create a ChromatinAssay using counts, features, fragments and annotations.







NoteAnswer








R

## - Create Chromatin Assay
assay <- Signac::CreateChromatinAssay(
    counts = cnts,
    ranges = features,
    fragments = fragments_file,
    annotation = annotations,
    genome = "hg19",
    min.cells = 10,
    min.features = 10
)
assay






What are the dimensions of this object? Are they comparable to the count matrix? Comment.







NoteAnswer








R

dim(cnts)
dim(assay)









It’s finally time to wrap the ChromatinAssay into a Seurat standard object! This is done using the CreateSeuratObject.







NoteQuestion



Create a Seurat object from the ChromatinAssay object.







NoteAnswer








R

## - Create Seurat object
PBMC <- Seurat::CreateSeuratObject(
    counts = assay,
    assay = 'ATAC',
    meta.data = metadata[metadata$is__cell_barcode == 1, ]
)
PBMC

PBMC[['ATAC']]
granges(PBMC)
Annotation(PBMC)










13.1.4 Check QCs

13.1.4.1 Cell-based QCs
The fraction of reads in peaks (FRiP) is a good indicator of how well each cell was handled during scATACseq processing.



R

PBMC$FRiP <- PBMC$peak_region_fragments / PBMC$passed_filters
PBMC$nCount_ATAC <- colSums(GetAssayData(PBMC, layer = "counts"))
PBMC$nFeature_ATAC <- colSums(GetAssayData(PBMC, layer = "counts") > 0)

quantile(PBMC$FRiP, seq(0, 1, 0.1))
quantile(PBMC$nCount_ATAC, seq(0, 1, 0.1))
quantile(PBMC$nFeature_ATAC, seq(0, 1, 0.1))



13.1.4.2 Peaks-based QCs







NoteQuestion



Which analysis are the fragments required for, exactly?
Could we still perform normalization/clustering/annotation without them? And motif enrichment analysis?
Since we do have the fragments file at hand, most of the QC steps are available (e.g. TSSEnrichment, NucleosomeSignal or fragment size distribution). Let’s go through them one by one.







NoteAnswer








R

# compute nucleosome signal score per cell
PBMC <- NucleosomeSignal(object = PBMC)
PBMC

# compute TSS enrichment score per cell
PBMC <- Signac::TSSEnrichment(object = PBMC, fast = FALSE)
PBMC









The TSSPlot function from Signac can be used to plot the fragment count per peak ~ TSS enrichment.



R

PBMC$high.tss <- ifelse(PBMC$TSS.enrichment > 3.5, 'High', 'Low')
TSSPlot(PBMC, group.by = 'high.tss') + NoLegend()
PBMC$high.tss <- ifelse(PBMC$TSS.enrichment > 2.5, 'High', 'Low')
TSSPlot(PBMC, group.by = 'high.tss') + NoLegend()


The FragmentHistogram function from Signac can be used to plot the fragment size distribution in peaks with different nucleosome signals.







NoteQuestion



Group genomic loci by their nucleosome signal (> 4 or < 4) and plot the fragment size distribution.







NoteAnswer








R

PBMC$nucleosome_group <- ifelse(PBMC$nucleosome_signal > 4, 'NS > 4', 'NS < 4')
FragmentHistogram(object = PBMC, group.by = 'nucleosome_group')










13.1.5 Filter cells and features
Just like standard scRNAseq data, scATACseq data needs to be filtered to remove low-quality cells and peaks.







NoteQuestion



Filter the Seurat object (cells and features) as deemed appropriate.







NoteAnswer








R

## - Filter data
PBMC <- subset(PBMC, subset = nCount_ATAC > 3000 & nCount_ATAC < 100000)
PBMC <- subset(PBMC, subset = nFeature_ATAC > 1000 & nFeature_ATAC < 20000)
PBMC <- subset(PBMC, subset = FRiP > 0.30)
PBMC <- subset(PBMC, subset = TSS.enrichment > 2.5 & nucleosome_signal < 4)
PBMC

## - Remove peaks with low coverage
PBMC <- PBMC[rowSums(GetAssayData(PBMC, layer = "counts")) > 10, ]
PBMC <- PBMC[rowSums(GetAssayData(PBMC, layer = "counts") > 0) > 10, ]
PBMC










13.1.6 Dimensionality reduction and clustering
Now that the dataset is filtered, we can proceed to data normalization, dimensionality reduction and clustering. Compared to scRNAseq, scATACseq data is much sparser and has a higher dimensionality. This has important implications for the choice of normalization and dimensionality reduction methods. scATACseq data are generally normalized using a TF-IDF normalization, which is implemented in the RunTFIDF function in Signac, and dimensionality reduction is performed using LSI (Latent Semantic Indexing) implemented in the RunSVD function.







NoteQuestion



Normalize then further reduce the dimensionality for visualization purposes.







NoteAnswer








R

## - Normalize data
PBMC <- RunTFIDF(PBMC)

## - Reduce dimensionality
PBMC <- FindTopFeatures(PBMC, min.cutoff = 'q50')
PBMC <- RunSVD(PBMC)

## - The first LSI component is often correlated with sequencing depth
DepthCor(PBMC)

## - Embed in 2D UMAP
PBMC <- RunUMAP(object = PBMC, reduction = 'lsi', dims = 2:30)

## - Cluster cells
PBMC <- FindNeighbors(object = PBMC, reduction = 'lsi', dims = 2:30)
PBMC <- FindClusters(object = PBMC, verbose = FALSE, algorithm = 3)

## - Visualize data
DimPlot(PBMC, label = TRUE) + NoLegend()






What can you observe in the UMAP projection of the dataset? Comment on the separation of some cell types into different spatially-resolved clusters.
crumbs: 13  Lab 7: Single-cell ATAC-seq analysis workflow

title: 13  Lab 7: Single-cell ATAC-seq analysis workflow
text:
13.2 Compute gene activity scores
Signac’s GeneActivity() function require scATACseq fragment information. Since we have them, we can estimate a gene activity score for each gene in the annotations.



R

gene.activities <- GeneActivity(PBMC)


We can now save this new object as an Assay in the PBMC object and normalize it.



R

PBMC[['RNA']] <- CreateAssayObject(counts = gene.activities)

# - Normalize the new RNA assay.
PBMC <- NormalizeData(
    object = PBMC,
    assay = 'RNA',
    normalization.method = 'LogNormalize',
    scale.factor = median(PBMC$nCount_RNA)
)
PBMC


One can now visualize expression of individual markers across clusters to infer cluster identity.







NoteQuestion



Assess the expression of known markers across clusters, projecting the cells in a 2D UMAP.







NoteAnswer








R

DefaultAssay(PBMC) <- 'RNA'
VlnPlot(
  object = PBMC,
  features = c(
    'MS4A1', # B-cell
    'CD3D', # T-cell
    'NKG7', # NK cell
    'TREM1' # Monocytes
  )
)
FeaturePlot(
  object = PBMC,
  features = c('MS4A1', 'CD3D', 'NKG7', 'TREM1'),
  max.cutoff = 'q95'
)


Based on these markers, we can annotate clusters. Note that the cluster numbers obtained in your session may differ from the ones below: adapt the mapping to your own results!



R

PBMC$annotation <- dplyr::case_when(
  Idents(PBMC) %in% c(0, 5, 9, 12) ~ "Monocytes",
  Idents(PBMC) %in% c(1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 10) ~ "T-cells",
  Idents(PBMC) %in% c(6) ~ "NK-cells",
  Idents(PBMC) %in% c(8, 11) ~ "B-cells",
  Idents(PBMC) %in% c(13, 14) ~ "DC"
)
DimPlot(PBMC, group.by = 'annotation', label = TRUE) + NoLegend()

title: 13  Lab 7: Single-cell ATAC-seq analysis workflow
section: 13.3 Find peaks differentially accessible across clusters
text:
13.3 Find peaks differentially accessible across clusters
Finally, we can perform differential peak accessibility analysis to identify peaks that are differentially accessible between clusters. This is done using the FindMarkers function from Seurat, run on the ATAC assay.



R

DefaultAssay(PBMC) <- 'ATAC'
Idents(PBMC) <- PBMC$annotation
da_peaks <- FindMarkers(
  object = PBMC,
  ident.1 = "Monocytes",
  ident.2 = "B-cells",
  test.use = 'LR',
  latent.vars = 'nCount_ATAC'
)
head(da_peaks)
VlnPlot(
  object = PBMC,
  features = rownames(da_peaks)[1],
  pt.size = 0.1,
  idents = c("Monocytes","B-cells")
)
CoveragePlot(
  object = PBMC,
  region = rownames(da_peaks)[1],
  extend.upstream = 10000,
  extend.downstream = 10000
)

text: 15.1 Process testis data in R

title: 15  Lab 8: Pseudotime analyses
text:
15.1.1 Import testis data from GSE112013 and pre-process it
We will work on a testis dataset, from the “The adult human testis transcriptional cell atlas” study (Guo et al., Cell Research 2018). This dataset contains single-cell RNAseq data from human testis. It is available on the GEO database under the accession number GSE112013.
We have applied the different analysis steps we have learned over the past three days to the count matrix GSE112013_Combined_UMI_table.txt.gz. See the code below for the details of pre-processing steps, and run it in your session (this takes a few minutes, and requires ~8 GB of memory).







Note👀 Data pre-processing 👇





Check the GEO page for supplementary processed data, and download the GSE112013_Combined_UMI_table.txt.gz table.
With this data, we will:

Import the dataset in R as a SingleCellExperiment object,
Remove doublets,
Filter genes and cells,
Normalize counts,
Correct for batch effect,
Cluster cells.




R

library(SingleCellExperiment)

# Create SingleCellExperiment object

rm(x); invisible(gc())

    assays = list(counts = counts),
    colData = DataFrame(cellid = colnames(counts))
)

testis$donor <- str_replace(testis$cellid, '-.*', '')
testis$replicate <- str_replace(testis$cellid, '.*-', '')

table(testis$donor, testis$replicate)

##    Donor1 1000 1248
##    Donor2  985 1009
##    Donor3 1116 1132

# Remove doublets

  |

##  singlet doublet 
##     6224     266
testis <- testis[, testis$scDblFinder.class == 'singlet']

    org.Hs.eg.db::org.Hs.eg.db,
    keys = rownames(testis), keytype = 'SYMBOL',
    columns = c('ENSEMBL', 'GENETYPE')
) |>
    filter(GENETYPE == 'protein-coding') |>
    distinct(SYMBOL, .keep_all = TRUE)
##  
##  'select()' returned 1:many mapping between keys and columns

rowData(testis)$gene_id <- gene_info$ENSEMBL

testis <- scrapper::quickRnaQc.se(testis, subsets = list(mito = mito), block = testis$sample)

    testis, size.factors = sizeFactors(testis), block = testis$sample,
    more.norm.args = list(delayed = FALSE)
)

    batch = testis$donor,

)

title: 15  Lab 8: Pseudotime analyses
text:
15.2 Trajectory inference (TI) in scRNAseq
An important question in scRNAseq field of research is: how to identify a cell trajectory from high-dimensional expression data and map individual cells onto it? A large number of methods have currently emerged, each one with their own specificities, assumptions, and strengths. A nice breakdown (from 2019, so already very outdated!) is available from Saelens et al., Nat. Biotech. 2019 (doi: 10.1038/s41587-019-0071-9):


15.2.1 Trajectory
Slingshot is perhaps one of the most widely used algorithms for users who want to focus on R-based approaches.







NoteQuestion



Read Slingshot documentation to understand how to identify lineages in a scRNAseq dataset in R.
Why is it recommended to infer lineages from PCA space rather than t-SNE or UMAP space, even though these spaces do “reveal” an obvious trajectory in 2D?
Infer lineages, using cluster annotations as information to build the MST. Note that you will first need to remove the 50th dimension of the corrected embedding for slingshot to work (bug reported).







NoteAnswer








R

reducedDim(germcells, 'corrected_2') <- reducedDim(germcells, 'corrected')[, 1:49]
germcells_slingshot <- slingshot::slingshot(
    germcells,
    reducedDim = 'corrected_2',
    clusterLabels = germcells$annotation
)
slingshot::slingLineages(germcells_slingshot)
##  $Lineage1
##  [1] "late spermatids"                "early spermatids"              
##  [3] "late primary spermatocytes"     "early primary spermatocytes"   
##  [5] "differentiating spermatogonia"  "undifferentiated spermatogonia"










15.2.2 Pseudotime
slingshot automatically deduces a pseudotime for each cell, based on the inferred lineage. It can be useful to visualize the trajectory of cells in a 2D space, and to order cells along the trajectory.







NoteQuestion



Recover pseudotime values and principal curves from slingshot output.







NoteAnswer








R

# Fetching pseudotime
germcells$pseudotime <- slingshot::slingPseudotime(germcells_slingshot)[, 'Lineage1']

# Fetching principal curve in PCA space
pca_curve <- slingshot::slingCurves(germcells_slingshot, as.df = TRUE)
colnames(pca_curve)

##  [15] "Dim.15"  "Dim.16"  "Dim.17"  "Dim.18"  "Dim.19"  "Dim.20"  "Dim.21"

##  [43] "Dim.43"  "Dim.44"  "Dim.45"  "Dim.46"  "Dim.47"  "Dim.48"  "Dim.49" 
##  [50] "Order"   "Lineage"
## Rename the coordinates columns (all but the last two, `Order` and `Lineage`)

##  3 0.3128256 0.1697593     3       1
##  4 0.3149677 0.1670916     4       1
##  5 0.3171095 0.1644158     5       1
##  6 0.3192504 0.1617224     6       1






We would like to visualize the trajectory of cells in our TSNE space, but the principal curve is only available in PCA space. We can use slingshot to embed it in the TSNE space!







NoteAnswer








R

tsne_curve <- slingshot::embedCurves(germcells_slingshot, 'TSNE', smoother = 'loess', span = 0.1) |>
    slingshot::slingCurves(as.df = TRUE)
tsne_curve <- tsne_curve[order(tsne_curve$Order), ]
head(tsne_curve)
##                                TSNE1     TSNE2 Order Lineage
##  Donor1-CGACCTTGTAGCGTCC-2 -9.962902 -32.59378     1       1
##  Donor1-GTGTGCGGTGGAAAGA-1 -9.962902 -32.59378     2       1
##  Donor1-GTTAAGCGTTTGACTG-1 -9.962902 -32.59378     3       1
##  Donor1-CGGACACTCAGCAACT-1 -9.962902 -32.59378     4       1
##  Donor1-CGCTTCATCTAACTGG-1 -9.962902 -32.59378     5       1
##  Donor1-TCATTTGTCTTGGGTA-1 -9.962902 -32.59378     6       1






Plot PCA and tSNE embeddings, coloring cells by either their annotation or their pseudotime value. Overlay the principal curves to each embedding.







NoteAnswer








R

df <- tibble(
    PC1 = reducedDim(germcells, 'corrected')[,1],
    PC2 = reducedDim(germcells, 'corrected')[,2],
    TSNE1 = reducedDim(germcells, 'TSNE')[,1],
    TSNE2 = reducedDim(germcells, 'TSNE')[,2],
    annotation = germcells$annotation,
    pseudotime = germcells$pseudotime
)
cowplot::plot_grid(
    df |>
        ggplot() +
        geom_point(aes(PC1, PC2, col = annotation)) +
        geom_path(data = pca_curve |> filter(Lineage == 1), aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
        theme_bw() +
        coord_fixed(),
    df |>
        ggplot() +
        geom_point(aes(TSNE1, TSNE2, col = annotation)) +
        geom_path(data = tsne_curve |> filter(Lineage == 1), aes(x = TSNE1, y = TSNE2)) +
        theme_bw() +
        coord_fixed(),
    df |>
        ggplot() +
        geom_point(aes(PC1, PC2, col = pseudotime)) +
        geom_path(data = pca_curve |> filter(Lineage == 1), aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
        theme_bw() +
        coord_fixed(),
    df |>
        ggplot() +
        geom_point(aes(TSNE1, TSNE2, col = pseudotime)) +
        geom_path(data = tsne_curve |> filter(Lineage == 1), aes(x = TSNE1, y = TSNE2)) +
        theme_bw() +
        coord_fixed()
)






















NoteQuestion



Check the distribution of pseudotime values across the different cell clusters.
What do you observe? Where you expecting this?







NoteAnswer








R

tibble(
    annotation = germcells$annotation,
    pseudotime = germcells$pseudotime
) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = annotation, y = pseudotime, fill = annotation)) +
    geom_violin(scale = 'width') +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NULL, width = 0.1, fill = 'white') +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1))












slingshot does not know in which direction cells differentiate: the pseudotime may well increase from late spermatids to spermatogonia! Correct pseudotime values, so that they increase along the differentiation. Note that the start.clus argument of slingshot() can also be used to specify the starting point of a trajectory.



R

pt <- slingshot::slingPseudotime(germcells_slingshot)[, 'Lineage1']
first_type <- levels(germcells$annotation)[1]
last_type <- rev(levels(germcells$annotation))[1]
if (median(pt[germcells$annotation == first_type], na.rm = TRUE) > median(pt[germcells$annotation == last_type], na.rm = TRUE)) {
    pt <- -1 * pt
}
germcells$pseudotime <- scales::rescale(pt, c(0, 1))






15.2.3 BONUS: Daunting snippet but that makes a cool figure for a paper: modeling pseudotime-dependent gene expression
Using pseudotime / cell, one can model gene expression along the differentiation process. This alleviates the need to study gene expression per cell, and allows one to focus on process-related effects (e.g. gene expression during a developmental trajectory).







NoteQuestion



Try to do so for few markers of spermatogonia, spermatocytes and spermatids.







NoteAnswer








R

genes <- c('ID4', 'SYCP3', 'DMC1', 'ACR', 'PRM1', 'PGK2')
fitExprs <- logcounts(germcells[genes, ]) |> # ----------------------------------- Get norm. counts for genes of interest
    as.matrix() |>
    t() |>
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(  # ----------------------------------------------------------------- Add information for each cell
        cellID = colnames(germcells),
        annotation = germcells$annotation,
        pseudotime = germcells$pseudotime
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(pseudotime)) |>
    pivot_longer(all_of(genes), names_to = 'gene', values_to = 'obs_expr') |> # - Pivot in "long" tidy format
    mutate(gene = factor(gene, genes)) |>
    group_by(gene) |> # ------------------------------------------------------- Group rows by genes
    nest() |> # --------------------------------------------------------------- For each gene, extract the subtable into a column named data
    mutate(
        gamModel = map(data, ~mgcv::gam(obs_expr ~ s(pseudotime, bs = "cs"), data = .)),
        gamFitted_expr = map(gamModel, predict) # ------------------------------ For each gene, fit the expression values ~ pseudotime with a GAM
    ) |>
    dplyr::select(-ends_with('Model')) |>
    unnest(c(data, ends_with('_expr'))) # -------------------------------------- Unnest all the modelled expressions
ggplot(fitExprs) +
    geom_point(aes(x = pseudotime, y = obs_expr, col = annotation), alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_line(aes(x = pseudotime, y = gamFitted_expr), col = 'white', linewidth = 2, alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_line(aes(x = pseudotime, y = gamFitted_expr), col = '#af2d0c', linewidth = 1) +
    theme_bw() +
    facet_grid(gene~., scales = 'free') +
    labs(y = 'logcounts') +
    ggtitle('Fitted models of pseudotime-dependent gene expression')

title: 15  Lab 8: Pseudotime analyses
text:
15.3 Ordering trajectory with RNA velocity
As we saw earlier, TI does not necessarily know which direction is right for a given trajectory. This orientation can be sometimes refined using RNA velocity. Let’s see whether RNA velocity helps orientating our spermatocyte differentiation lineage trajectory here.






WarningSpliced and unspliced counts



RNA velocity requires the counts of spliced and unspliced reads, for each gene in each cell. These counts are not provided in GEO: they were computed from the raw reads of the study with velocyto, and the resulting loom file (Guo_testis_full-counts.loom) will be made available by your instructors during the workshop. The code below is therefore not run when the book is built.









NoteQuestion




Read velociraptor documentation. What do you need to compute RNA velocity scores in R?
Import spliced and unspliced counts computed with velocyto in R.
Try and compute RNA velocity.








NoteAnswer








R

## - Import entire GSE112013 dataset with spliced/unspliced counts
full_GSE112013_counts <- LoomExperiment::import('Guo_testis_full-counts.loom')
full_GSE112013_counts

## - Filter `germcells` genes and cells to only retain those present in `full_GSE112013_counts`
germcells <- germcells[
    rowData(germcells)$gene_id %in% rowData(full_GSE112013_counts)$Accession,
    germcells$Barcode %in% full_GSE112013_counts$Barcode
]

## - Reorder rows of `full_GSE112013_counts_germcells` to match those of `germcells`
full_GSE112013_counts_germcells <- full_GSE112013_counts[match(rowData(germcells)$gene_id, rowData(full_GSE112013_counts)$Accession), match(germcells$Barcode, full_GSE112013_counts$Barcode)]
dim(germcells)
dim(full_GSE112013_counts_germcells)

## - Add spliced/unspliced counts to germcells
assay(germcells, 'spliced', withDimnames=FALSE) <- as(assay(full_GSE112013_counts_germcells, 'spliced'), 'dgCMatrix')
assay(germcells, 'unspliced', withDimnames=FALSE) <- as(assay(full_GSE112013_counts_germcells, 'unspliced'), 'dgCMatrix')
germcells

## - Run velociraptor
velo_out <- velociraptor::scvelo(
    germcells,
    assay.X = "counts",
    subset.row = rowData(germcells)$isHVG,
    use.dimred = "corrected"
)
velo_out










Embed the velocity field in tSNE scRNAseq embedding and plot the RNA velocity field on top of tSNE projection. Conclude.




R

embedded_velo <- velociraptor::embedVelocity(reducedDim(germcells, "TSNE"), velo_out)
head(embedded_velo)
grid_df <- velociraptor::gridVectors(reducedDim(germcells, "TSNE"), embedded_velo, resolution = 30, scale = TRUE)
head(grid_df)
scater::plotReducedDim(germcells, 'TSNE', colour_by = "annotation", point_alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_segment(
        data = grid_df,
        mapping = aes(x = start.1, y = start.2, xend = end.1, yend = end.2),
        arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.05, "inches"), type = "closed")
    )

title: 16  Group projects
text:
16.1 Choose a dataset
Each group picks one dataset. It can be a dataset from your own research, a dataset from a paper you like, or one of the many datasets distributed by the scRNAseq package:
R

library(scRNAseq)
datasets <- surveyDatasets()
datasets
searchDatasets("pancreas")
sce <- fetchDataset("baron-pancreas-2016", "2023-12-14", path = "human")
The CZ CELLxGENE Discover and Human Cell Atlas portals, as well as GEO, are other good places to find processed count matrices.

title: 16  Group projects
text:
16.2 Analyse it
Here is a checklist of the analysis steps we covered during the week. Not all of them will be relevant to your dataset: decide which ones are, and why.

Import the data into a SingleCellExperiment object (Lab 3, Lab 4)
Quality control and filtering of cells and genes (Lab 4)
Normalization, feature selection and dimensionality reduction (Lab 5)
Batch correction, if required (Lab 6)
Clustering, marker genes and cell annotation (Lab 5)
Differential expression analysis between conditions, with pseudobulk (Lab 6)
Trajectory inference and pseudotime, if relevant (Lab 8)

title: 16  Group projects
text:
16.3 Present it
Prepare a short presentation (10 minutes, max 5 slides), covering:


What: what is the biological question, and what is the dataset?

Why: why is single-cell RNA-seq relevant to answer this question?

Where / When / How: which analysis steps did you perform, and which choices did you make?

Conclusions: what did you learn, and what would you do next?
